subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

speechtext:
Mr. G. E. Halpenny (London) presented the first report of the special committee on defence expenditures, and moved that the report be concurred in.
Motion agreed to.
On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Acting Prime Minister. In view of press reports from Paris, will the government make known to the United Kingdom, the United States and France its view that the ban on nuclear tests should be discussed and, if possible, decided at the forthcoming summit conference?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Leader of the Opposition for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. I have not seen the press reports to which the hon. gentleman refers. However, sir, it is well known that disarmament is to be an important item on the agenda of the summit meetings, and there is obviously a close connection between the question of the discontinuance of nuclear tests and disarmament.
On the question of nuclear tests, the policy of the Canadian government has been made very clear, both in public and in private, to our allies, including the countries to which the hon. gentleman referred in his question, on many previous occasions. Therefore I do not think there can be any doubt in the minds of any of our allies as to the government's firm opposition to the continuance of such tests.
On the orders of the day:

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF WORK ON BOMARC SITE AND SAGE CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. In view of the
understandable confusion at the moment and, I might add, the genuine concern of the people of my area, can the minister say, first, whether work will be proceeded with as planned at the Bomarc site near North Bay? Second, regardless of the success or failure of the Bomarc, will the control project, which for security reasons is referred to as the defence installation at Trout lake, be continued without interruption?
Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National
Defence): On December 14 last, Mr. Speaker, a contract for some $3 million was let for the construction of the Bomarc site at North Bay. To date something over $427,000 has already been spent. It is not the intention of the government at the present time to cancel that contract. Work is proceeding and will continue to proceed until the government of the United States inform us of any change of program they may suggest in connection with the Bomarc development and the air defence plans for the defence of this continent.
Regarding the other installation which has been referred to, as the hon. gentleman said, as a defence installation, the purpose of that has not been declared for security reasons, but I see no reason why it could not now be announced that that is a SAGE communication centre. The SAGE communication system is designed not only to control the Bomarc but to control interceptors or any other weapons which are being used in the air defence system. It is of assistance in the identification and tracking of friendly and hostile aircraft, and may be described as a centre for air battle management and air surveillance. So, quite irrespective of what is the final decision regarding the Bomarc program, the SAGE program near North Bay will continue according to the present plans of the government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF WORK ON BOMARC SITE AND SAGE CENTRE
speechtext:
I should like to ask a supplementary question of the Minister of National Defence. In view of his reply that there will be no change in the Canadian program until the United States government has declared its position, continued, confirmed or changed, then may I ask the minister whether the government of Canada, since the announcement of the congressional committee on Friday last, has taken any steps whatever to ascertain what is the position of the government of the United States with regard to this matter at this time.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice, notice of which was given to him. Has the minister's attention been drawn to a statement made by Premier Smallwood in the Newfoundland house of assembly on April 25, in which Mr. Smallwood gives a summary of a conversation he says he had with the Minister of Justice last year on the subject of the proclamation of the Newfoundland legislation creating the position of a fourth judge in that province?
Second, was there such a conversation and, if so, did the minister decline to give an assurance regarding Newfoundland traditions, as alleged by Mr. Smallwood?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulion (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Smallwood-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for any unintentional discourtesy. Mr. Smallwood and I did have a conversation on this matter in his office, in June of last year, I think. Mr. Smallwood is an interesting man and it

was an. interesting and informal conversation, but it did not really go at all in the way or to the effect that he now seeks to convey.
There was no discussion of "traditions" in the sense in which ordinary people would understand that word. What actually happened was that Mr. Smallwood raised a number of specific points and made clear to me a number of his own views on them as to particular tests that should be applied in determining the qualifications of any person for appointment to this position. What he asked for was an assurance that the government of Canada would agree to accept his views as to these qualifications in making the appointment. He said that if we would give him this assurance he would call a cabinet meeting at once and proclaim the Newfoundland act.
I told Mr. Smallwood that in making appointments to the bench the government of Canada accepts no such restrictions as he sought to impose, and that I declined to enter into the improper bargain which he asked me to make. I simply told him that the government of Canada was ready, as soon as he proclaimed his act, to consider immediately the appointment of the best qualified man.
That is still our position today. We do not enter into bargains with respect to judicial appointments.
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is there any legislation of this parliament that would permit the minister to recommend such an appointment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not at the moment, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING NEWSPAPER ARTICLE ON INTERVIEW

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING NEWSPAPER ARTICLE ON INTERVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in two parts, stemming from statements in the morning press today by a Mr. Goldberg which say that the minister's review of his interviews with Mr. Goldberg in Moscow, given in this house last week, deformed the facts. First, has the minister any comment on this commentary upon the statement he gave us? Second, has he considered moving in this house to have Mr. Goldberg or the senior representative of the Associated Press in this country called before the bar of the house to explain his reflections upon the minister's veracity?
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING NEWSPAPER ARTICLE ON INTERVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not given consideration to the second suggestion as yet. With regard to the first part of the hon. member's question, I have seen the article to which reference is made. The account I saw in the Gazette was largely a reprint of the statements which I declared on Monday to be false, and I so declare again.
I notice there is very little comment by Mr. Goldberg except the flat statement that I have been incorrect in what I have said. The rest of it is a somewhat garbled account, in my opinion, as to statements which have already been dealt with. I had rather wondered why, if there was to be a reprint of this statement, a reprint of my statement might not have been made at the same time.
I notice that the correspondent, Mr. Goldberg, was misquoted in his original dispatch. This is, of course, a calamity. The word "if" was altered to "and" through a transmission error between Moscow and the Associated Press office in New York. I sympathize with him in the misquotation which occurred.
I notice that at the request of the Canadian Press, the Associated Press checked Goldberg on the accuracy of his original statement at the time; they were able to get in touch with him, and apparently he was able to reply. I notice that in the article, in justice to Mr. Goldberg, "the following facts have to be made known", and the following facts are a reprint of the original article.
I notice that Mr. Goldberg has had 27 years' experience. By inference I have had none. I notice that he was stationed in Paris, in Prague and at the United Nations; he has been abroad. I was stationed abroad for six years in France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and the United Kingdom. Mr. Goldberg's opinion is to be relied upon, apparently, because he was a war correspondent. I never had that privilege, Mr. Speaker. I was not a war correspondent. Many of them saw considerable danger in the course of their activities. My experience, unfortunately, was limited to just 20 battles.
I notice that in this article Mr. Goldberg attempts to implicate a distinguished civil servant, and accuses him of levity in the course of the discussion on uranium. The discussion on uranium consisted of one question. The distinguished civil servant is a very competent civil servant, Mr. Warren, assistant deputy minister of the Department of Trade and Commerce. He was not a war correspondent; he was just an officer in the Royal Canadian Navy who underwent as much danger and extreme hazards as any person in the Canadian navy.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Mr. Goldberg has left unexplained four things; the motive for his question; his original dispatch, which any reasonable person would assume was such to cause international trouble. He has left unexplained the fact that he asked no questions at the press conference; and he has left unexplained his reference to Blind River uranium, which is an uncommon expression nowadays because we speak of Elliot Lake, Bancroft, Beaver-lodge and Northwest Territories. I have noted the report in the paper, and I stand by my statement of Monday.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING NEWSPAPER ARTICLE ON INTERVIEW
speechtext:
May I ask a
supplementary question of the minister. Could the minister tell the house how many times since 1957 he has complained of being misquoted?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING NEWSPAPER ARTICLE ON INTERVIEW
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member is asking a question which is intended to be argumentative rather than one seeking information.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING NEWSPAPER ARTICLE ON INTERVIEW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in his statement of privilege last week the minister expressed surprise that no Canadian newspaper had tried to get in touch with him. Has it been brought to his attention that two Canadian newspapers did try to get in touch with him in Moscow and were unable to contact him?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING NEWSPAPER ARTICLE ON INTERVIEW
speechtext:
I received a note from the press gallery the day I spoke saying that some hours had been spent trying to get in contact with me in Moscow. I also received a telegram to the effect that a phone call was put through to Moscow, but a reply came back that the Canadian embassy was closed.
The Canadian embassy is never without someone in the building. The upper part is occupied by the ambassador, and the lower part is comprised of offices; when the staff is absent there is a security guard in attendance at all times, and he answers the phone in an emergency. During the period in question, which according to the telegram I received was from eight o'clock on Saturday morning onward, which would be three o'clock Moscow time, I was in the hotel and could have been reached there had the operator got through. There was no question about my not being accessible. Mr. Goldberg was.
On the orders of the day:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether he is now in a position to answer the questions asked him on April 29 concerning uranium.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. These questions were asked during my absence on April 29. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) inquired about certain reports concerning action being proposed in Australia. These reports in the press have been noted, to the effect that the government of Australia has had proposed to it financial assistance to the uranium industry in that country either through subsidies or by stockpiling.
I have no indication that any action has been taken on that proposal. In view of the relatively high cost of Australian uranium production it is doubtful whether such financial assistance, if forthcoming, would make Australian uranium seriously competitive with that of the lower cost Canadian producers.
Then on the same day the hon. member for Ottawa West drew attention to the increase in production of uranium in the United States. During the calendar year 1959 the production of Canadian uranium was less than the production of the United States of America by some 500 tons. It is expected that the United States production will rise further during 1960, because certain mines are only now reaching their contract output.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY ST. CLAIR RIVER    AWARD OF CONTRACT FOR CUT-OFF BY U.S.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY ST. CLAIR RIVER    AWARD OF CONTRACT FOR CUT-OFF BY U.S.
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Can the minister comment on a report that a large contract has been awarded by the United States corps of engineers for construction of a new cut-off channel at the southeast bend in the St. Clair river, being part of a larger project in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway?
Would the minister also explain why, although this particular phase of the over-all project is located entirely in Canada, the contract should have been awarded by the United States corps of engineers?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY ST. CLAIR RIVER    AWARD OF CONTRACT FOR CUT-OFF BY U.S.
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question shortly before I entered the house.
I have not seen the article in question, but I have had officials of my department check into it. They have been in touch with the Department of External Affairs, who have advised us as follows. In the reach of the St. Clair river to which the hon. member has referred, an intergovernmental agreement was worked out whereby the improved

channel would be financed by funds appropriated by the United States congress. The work on this channel was to be shared between Canada and the United States, Canadian and United States contractors being given equal opportunity to bid, and Canadian and United States labour being employed as equally as possible.
When bids were called about two months ago, two contractors, one Canadian and one from the United States, submitted bids. They were accepted, and these two contractors will presumably be hiring workers from their respective countries so that the provisions of the agreement worked out between the governments whereby Canadian and United States labour will be employed in approximately equal numbers may be fulfilled.
The maintenance of this channel will be the responsibility of the Canadian government.

subtopic: REPORTED DUMPING OF USED U.S. CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORTED DUMPING OF USED U.S. CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
May I
direct a question to the Minister of Defence Production. I have not given the hon. gentleman notice, but perhaps he can take this as notice if he desires. I should like to know whether the minister has seen an article which appeared in this morning's Gazette entitled "Dumping by U.S. Charged" which implies that millions of dollars worth of second hand United States construction equipment is being dumped in Canada with the sanction of the federal government.
Have representations been made to the minister against this action, as stated in the article, and has the hon. gentleman any comment to make thereon?

speakeroldname: Hon. Raymond O'Hurley (Minister of Defence Production):
subtopic: REPORTED DUMPING OF USED U.S. CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Laurier should know that sales of United States equipment have been going on for several years. Representations have been made with a view to the cancellation of the agreement under which these imports have been possible. I have been interested in this problem, and I do not think anybody approves of the dumping of used construction material on the Canadian market. On the other hand, while I was considering this brief, small contractors and municipal contractors as well as local municipalities, presented their views to the effect that it is to their advantage that this construction machinery be sold by crown assets to different municipalities in Canada. At the moment I am comparing the two briefs, one by this
Inquiries of the Ministry equipment company and the other by the municipalities and small contractors, and a decision will soon be reached by the government.
As I read the article, the Minister of Defence Production is said to have done a turn-about. There is no turn-about in this question, as the question has not been brought to the government. We are waiting for the preparation of the memorandum by small contractors, and especially municipal contractors.

subtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL-STATEMENT ON REPORTED SLAYING OF INMATE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL-STATEMENT ON REPORTED SLAYING OF INMATE
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Skeena asked me a supplementary question in connection with the death of an inmate at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary on Sunday. His supplementary question was a request for information as to where the physician was at the time the man fell and where he had to be called from.
I am advised that the doctor at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary is Dr. Lefebvre. He lives on Jean-Talon street in Montreal and is employed on a full time basis by the penitentiary. I am further advised that Dr. Lefebvre was called by the penitentiary between 10.15 and 10.20 a.m. on Sunday, May 1, and that he was informed that the penitentiary officials thought

Inquiries of the Ministry the inmate was already dead. He left immediately for the penitentiary, where he arrived between 10.40 and 10.45 a.m. In the meantime the inmate had been carried to the penitentiary hospital and had been looked after by the attendants and nurses. The death certificate was signed by the doctor at 10.50.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO FUND
speechtext: In view of the fact that as of March 31 the unemployment insurance fund had reached the alarmingly low figure of $359 million, can the Minister of Finance say whether he has, under the Unemployment Insurance Act, authorized any loans whatsoever by any agency of the government of Canada or otherwise to the unemployment insurance commission?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO FUND
speechtext: In thanking the hon. gentleman for his most generous and touching allusion, in reply may I say I recognize that I am replying to one of the greatest parliamentarians to have represented the riding of Essex East in the last five years.

Mr. Speaker, before calling it ten o'clock last night I had endeavoured to show that the economic ills of the maritime provinces can be directly attributed to three causes. These three causes are, first, the political union between the maritime provinces and the central provinces; second, the failure of the central provinces to carry out certain parts of their agreements included in the terms of union and their tardiness in carrying out other parts of their agreements; third, federal policies since confederation, which have been geared to the political and economic requirements of the central provinces rather than to the economic needs of the maritime provinces.
It did not make economic sense for the maritime provinces to join up politically with central Canada. The channels of trade have always run north and south, and when these channels were changed to an east and west direction the result was that the maritime provinces were placed in an inferior economic position. However, out of loyalty to the British crown and to British traditions, they accepted that inferior position, knowing that it would cost them something financially but not knowing quite how much, and trusting that the central provinces, in good faith, would see to it that this price would be kept to the absolute minimum.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw a parallel between the maritime provinces and Newfoundland. If it made poor sense for the maritime provinces to join central Canada, it made even less economic sense for Newfoundland to become a part of Canada. All our production is competitive with mainland Canada. None of our production is complementary to mainland Canada. A celebrated economist pointed out that analogy a few days ago as between Canada and Russia, that

Canada and Russia have competitive production. If the maritime provinces made Canada possible, Newfoundland made Canada complete.
Now, had the maritime provinces put dollars before loyalty they would not have joined with the central provinces. They would very likely have formed a union amongst themselves, and quite possibly they might have joined with the United States. Had Newfoundland put dollars first we certainly would not have joined with Canada. We did not have to join with mainland Canada. We had excellent relations with our friends in the United States. They had already established bases in our country, and those bases were making a very big contribution to our economic life. Like every free people we were entitled to self-determination, and if we had been prepared to think only in economic terms our chances of development and prosperity as part of the United States would have been far greater than our chances as part of Canada.
But our loyalty in Newfoundland to the British crown and to British traditions is second to none, and like the maritimes we too were prepared to pay a price. Some hon. members may wonder why I make that statement. You will ask, is not Newfoundland better off now than ever before? The answer is yes, but Newfoundland was better off than ever before in her history before she joined Canada. As part of the United States-if we had made a request and elected to become a state of the United States-we would be eminently better off than we are at the present time.
I remember that when I first came here to parliament in the years 1949 and 1950, many of my colleagues would inquire as to how Newfoundland was getting on as part of Canada. I would say well, we are doing very well but, and as soon as I came to this word "but" I would seldom ever be permitted to go any further. As soon as I said "but" they would interrupt me and say, are you not getting family allowances; are you not getting old age pensions? Certainly we are. Since we are a part of Canada, what would be strange about that? Why would anybody ask that question?
This type of question reveals an attitude that seems to be imbedded in the subconscious minds of mainlanders. One overlooked it because one realized that they meant well and did not realize the type of attitude they were revealing. However, I believe it is worth while to examine the reason for that kind of attitude.
The price paid by the maritimes to become a part of Canada-and I think we can include
3, 1960

Over the years various ingenious methods have been devised to try to offset that situation to some extent. I have no quarrel with those methods that have been invented. They will have to be continued for many years to come. But I think we must realize that these methods have generated a wrong relationship. They have put the maritime provinces in the position of poor relations who have become permanent pensioners of the rest of Canada. It implies also an unwillingness to recognize the indebtedness of the rest of Canada to the maritime provinces and to Newfoundland, and because of that fact this assistance which is given in various forms is regarded by the people on the mainland of Canada as generosity, as a favour, as something emanating from their big-heartedness rather than something that is justly due.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
No. Every time you have asked me a question it has been a foolish one. I am not going to be interrupted.

answer it.
I think the ancient and decrepit member from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) had better remain quiet.

limited.

The first step toward curing these ills is a change of attitude and a recognition of the sacrifices made by the Atlantic provinces for a greater cause. Nowhere is that spirit more lacking than toward Newfoundland. We have been constantly reminded in the ten years of union of how much we are getting out of confederation. Never a word has been said publicly, nor has there been an acknowledgement by any official that I know of, as to how much Newfoundland contributed to Canada. That contribution included 150,000 square miles of new territory, rich resources in the Labrador, mineral wealth, hydroelectric power, half a million new citizens, an addition to the domestic market worth $250 million annually, international airports which greatly strengthen the bargaining power of Canada with other countries, various public services including railway services, hotels, public wharves and other public structures.
Last but not least, most important of all is the fact that union with Canada made

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces Canada a nation in the true and real sense of the word. We cannot appraise that in terms of dollars and cents, but if you want to put a value on it compare Canada with Newfoundland to what Canada would be if Newfoundland and Labrador were a part of the United States. There is never a word of appreciation of what we have given to Canada. The only reference is to the few million dollars received as a hand-out.
We are only human and we like a little appreciation, too. The first requirement, then, if we are going to tackle this problem of the maritimes is a new spirit and a new motive born of a sense of appreciation and a desire to end the disabilities from which the maritimes suffer. This new spirit is needed because it is going to involve sacrifice on the part of the other Canadian provinces. It is their turn now to accept the sacrifice for Canada. This means they may have to scale down the rate of some of their improvements in public services in order to raise the level of those in the maritimes. The economic rehabilitation of the maritime provinces should be a truly national project. It should be not merely a project of the federal government but a national project in the fullest sense of that word, undertaken and motivated by a desire in the hearts of Canadians in the other provinces to see the maritimes achieve economic equality.
This will involve a long term program, and I think this program should be based on two main principles. The first is equality of opportunity. The second principle is that there should be a minimum level of public services for all Canadians. That will require in the maritimes a survey of the existing services to determine what that level should be. Once that level of public services has been determined, then fiscal grants will have to be adjusted to attain that goal over a predetermined period. Equality of opportunity means an opportunity to help us to help ourselves. We do not want to be permanent pensioners existing on hand-outs. We can stand on our own feet. We have the resources which are able to supply us with a reasonable standard of living, but we do not have equality of opportunity at the present time. Tight money, high interest rates, excessive transportation costs, tariff policies and monetary policies all militate against the maritime provinces.
Ways and means must be found to offset those disabilities. The Maritime Freight Rates Act should be restored to its original proportions. Tariff policies should be adjusted to suit the needs of the industries. Tariff policies should be adjusted to provide special

incentives to new industry. Tight money can be overcome by the setting up of a development corporation for the rehabilitation of our existing industries and the encouragement of new ones.
All these things are included in this amendment, either expressly or by implication. They have been included in the so-called Atlantic charter to which the Conservative members from the maritimes have subscribed. In view of that fact it is difficult to see how they can vote against this amendment. The blueprint for the Atlantic provinces has been set forth in very great detail in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald and there is no need to elaborate further on that point. All that is necessary is to untie our hands, and we can do the rest.

Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I am very happy this afternoon to say a few words on this resolution. I do not intend to follow the argument of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, except to say that we in what were formerly called the maritime provinces are very happy and proud indeed to have the province of Newfoundland as one of our associates in the Atlantic area.
We are very happy, too, that at no time in its history did the old colony of Newfoundland show any intention or desire to belong to any other organized nation than those comprising the British empire or the British commonwealth. I can assure the hon. member that if he will go back and read the debates in the House of Commons at the time Newfoundland came into confederation, he will find no stronger advocates for the union than those who were then in opposition and who belonged to the Conservative party. I sometimes feel that we get very little credit for this from Newfoundland, and that we are held out as great opponents of Newfoundland and its prosperity and happiness. I can assure you that this was never the case.
The hon. member did say that Newfoundland has not received very much from confederation.
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I did not make that statement; the hon. gentleman must have misunderstood me. I admit what we have received; I do not want there to be any doubt about that.

Then I stand corrected. But I did hear the hon. gentleman say that perhaps we did not give a proper balance to what Newfoundland had contributed to Canada compared with what Newfoundland received from the other parts of Canada.
Yes.

I was interested to see the other day a statement by Premier Smallwood to the effect that the day on which Newfoundland entered confederation was one of the greatest days in the history of that province. He was opening, I think, the new provincial building in the city of St. John's.
Mr. Speaker, it has been said that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) has had considerable courage in opening up this matter of the maritime and Atlantic provinces. The subject has already been fairly well discussed by members on both sides of the house. As I listened to the speeches of hon. members on the other side I must say that I found the facts certainly had no resemblance to the material in the speeches made by those hon. members. It has 79951-0-221
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces been amusing indeed to listen to these speeches filled with gloomy forebodings about conditions in the different Atlantic provinces. I would recommend to my hon. friends in the opposition that they read some of the leading papers in the maritime provinces, that they read some of the special editions of those papers showing the new industries which are springing up almost weekly at the present time in different parts of those provinces. If I were in my own home town of Sussex this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, as I was invited to be, I would be assisting in opening a new industry. This has become quite characteristic of the different sections of my own province.
The feature about the Atlantic provinces which I am sure is worrying my hon. friends opposite most at the present time is the small number of Liberal representatives in this house from those provinces. There are no Liberal members from Nova Scotia. There are no Liberal members from the province of Prince Edward Island. We have a few from the province of New Brunswick. The three maritime provinces sent three Liberal members here in the last election.
As far as the provincial field is concerned today, all three maritime provinces, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, have Conservative governments. Therefore it is no wonder that on the eve of elections in the two provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, we hear a cry of desperation, as it were, on the part of the few Liberals who are here representing these provinces. Indeed I think it is quite significant, Mr. Speaker, that the attack on this government should come from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in the province of Newfoundland, because that province is the last outpost of Liberalism to be found anywhere in this country.
It is true that the maritime provinces have their problems. These are problems which have been accumulating for many years. The hon. member who just took his seat mentioned some of them. Our greatest problem has been that of geography, as everyone knows. After confederation we did not prosper in the maritime provinces as we had hoped to. As the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo says, we might have done better financially if we had thrown in our lot with the United States. But there was no sentiment, at least very little, for that move in those provinces at the time; and I would say, Mr. Speaker, that there is practically none today.
We have received a very great compliment in the resolution, which expresses what they consider is the hope that in three years'

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces time we the government could have and would have overcome the disabilities which our provinces suffered for years since confederation, and most of all the disabilities we suffered at the hands of the Liberal party in this country for 23 years.
The other day the hon. member spoke about the deserts of the maritime provinces and said that we had made our full contribution to the rest of Canada. I do not think there is anyone who can or would doubt that our people have made a tremendous contribution to Canada. In years past they went to all sections. The great west was opened up to a large extent by men from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. We also bore our share of the responsibility of opening up different parts of what we then called Upper and Lower Canada. So we feel that we have been very deserving as far as this country is concerned.
However, there have been two matters which have particularly reacted against our prosperity. As I mentioned a moment ago, geography was one of the great handicaps to our provinces. The railway situation and transportation was the great problem. The railway and transportation question is still a great problem for us. Shortly after confederation the Intercolonial railway was built, which was supposed to be a great help to our three provinces. I am not going into the history of railroads, but it is sufficient to say that on account of the long hauls the Intercolonial railway did not provide the opportunities we had hoped.
In 1914 it was found that the situation had become practically intolerable as far as transportation was concerned. From 1914 to 1927 the situation went from bad to worse. In 1927, on the recommendation of Sir Rae Duncan, father of the Duncan report, the Maritime Freight Rates Act was brought into being. From 1927 to the present time freight rates have been increasing horizontally across this country, mostly under Liberal governments, I may say, until the situation in the maritime provinces had become absolutely intolerable.
Hon. members opposite ask us, what are you doing about the situation at the present time? Well, a good physician or a good doctor always examines the patient very carefully to find out just what the situation is. The present government has appointed a royal commission to study and report on the situation in the Atlantic provinces. That report has not been brought in as yet, but I am satisfied that when it is brought in this great problem of transportation as far as our part of the country is concerned will receive very careful attention.

May I say that in my opinion the Maritime Freight Rates Act must be brought up to date; it must reflect the benefits to which the Atlantic provinces are entitled. We must not again be neglected for so many years under a transportation system such as we have had in the past if we are really to play a proper part in confederation.
Would the minister permit a question? Would he say what government was in office when the Maritime Freight Rates Act was enacted?
Does that make very much difference?
It makes a lot of difference to historians.

The Liberal government was in office then, and it was in office for most of the time since, when all the inequalities as a result of the horizontal increases came into effect.
The other great problem which I mentioned a moment ago was that of cheaper power. I have heard hon. members from New Brunswick and other parts sneer at what has been done by this government to assist in the development of power in the province of New Brunswick. Beechwood has been mentioned many times in this house; it was mentioned many times before the present government came into power, and even before the Flemming government came into power in New Brunswick.
The facts are these. For many months the premier of New Brunswick came to Ottawa and asked for assistance in order that power might be produced at Beechwood on the Saint John river. All he got was smiles; no promises. Finally in desperation the premier of New Brunswick, Hon. Hugh John Flemming, determined to take the matter into his own hands and, as we know-this is history now -he borrowed money from banks and wherever he could. He took great chances and displayed great courage. He started Beechwood, and until the present government came to power he received no assistance whatsoever from the federal parliament. After the present government came to power in 1957 a $30 million loan was made to the province to pay for the building of Beechwood, at a low interest rate of 3| per cent.
In what year?
Did the minister say 1957?

In 1959. In addition to the assistance the province received toward the construction of Beechwood we also received, as hon. members know, assistance toward the construction of thermal plants, the grid

system in New Brunswick and other maritime provinces, and so on. Perhaps I may be allowed to read an extract from a speech made by Hon. Hugh John Flemming in the provincial legislature. This is from the synoptic report. Speaking of Beechwood he had this to say:
Well, Mr. Speaker, the opposition leader does not realize what that loan meant to us. I have spoken in this house many times regarding our many trips to Ottawa between 1953 and 1958 when his party was in power there, in an attempt to secure some encouragement and some financial guarantee of our bonds in order to start the Beechwood project which we knew we needed, or rather would need very soon. We received politeness and courtesy from Mr. St. Laurent- nothing more-and, Mr. Speaker, you cannot start a $30 million project without something more substantial than politeness and courtesy. We finally started the project on our own resources and, Mr. Speaker, that took some faith and courage.
I emphasize that. It did take great faith and courage on the part of the premier of New Brunswick. The report continues:
The official opening was held in June 1955 and the St. Laurent Liberal federal government did share in it. They really did something. Perhaps they deserve some credit. They allowed the Right Hon. Mr. Howe to fly to Presque Isle, Maine, in his aeroplane, drive to Beechwood by motor car, and make a speech. But, Mr. Speaker, as I have said, the Beechwood hydro development project has been a magnificent success.
The report goes on to say, further on:
From the Liberals we received-politeness and courtesy and a speech by Mr. Howe.
From the present Conservative government we received a cheque for $29,500,000 at 31 per cent interest repayable over an eight-year period.
Hon. members can make their own comparisons.
What has happened as a result of this cheap power which we now have in my province? I apologize for speaking mainly about the province of New Brunswick, but the minister from Nova Scotia spoke of his own province yesterday and I think that I might therefore be excused for confining most of my remarks to New Brunswick. What has happened as a result of this cheaper power? I should like to quote from an article in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of February 9 of this year. The heading is "Plenty of Power for the Whole Area". It goes on to say:
Progress means more Industry. More Industry means more power, and that Is what the greater Saint John in the province of New Brunswick is getting.
That is a direct result of the efforts and the work of the federal government as far as my own province is concerned. Having that federal grant has helped the establishment of an oil refinery near Saint John, a $50 million project which could not and would not have been built if we did not have cheap 79951-0-221J
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces power as the result of assistance from the dominion government. Another article in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of December 2, 1959 speaks about the railway situation.
Says Fast Rail Service Helping Atlantic Ports
Faster Canadian National Railways services are placing the ports of Halifax and Saint John in a better position to increase their share of Canada's year-round export and import traffic, D. V. Gonder, vice president and general manager for the Atlantic region of the company, told an Atlantic ports day panel in Saint John, New Brunswick, Tuesday.
I have a long list of new enterprises which have sprung up and which are being built around the city of Saint John and in other parts of the province of New Brunswick at the present time. An airport addition contract has been awarded and a larger airport is being built near the city; new homes have set a record, says another article in a Saint John paper. If the people of the province of New Brunswick were discouraged why is it, as someone mentioned the other day, that the population of the province has greatly increased? It does not need me to tell this house that in days gone by we could hardly keep our average population in the maritime provinces on account of the fact that thousands of people left there every year. In the last few years, particularly in the last three years, the population of my province has grown very rapidly because the people of that province are willing to stay in New Brunswick, and they now have faith in their native province.
I am not going to weary the house with any more of these articles and headlines; I have a great many of them here. They all point to one thing, namely that the situation is improving and improving beneficially as far as our province is concerned.
How about primary industries? We heard the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robi-chaud) speak about the coal mines of Nova Scotia which have had a hard time. I know that this federal government has done everything that it is humanly possible for any government to do to assist. I would defy anyone to question that statement; but has the hon. member ever mentioned the coal mines in New Brunswick? Our coal mines have never been in a better position in the last 25 or 30 years than they are at the present time. We are producing about a million tons of coal, which is more than the normal amount we produce. We are not only producing it, Mr. Speaker, we are selling every ton of it and the employment of the miners in the Minto area is kept at a maximum.
So much for coal; I might ask, what assistance are we getting from the federal government? Yesterday, my colleague spoke

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces about the assistance in subventions, which has been a great help to the maritime provinces' coal industry. We also get great assistance in loans from the federal coal board, which has assisted the mining operators in Minto very greatly. There is splendid cooperation between the federal department and the department of mines in the province of New Brunswick.
What about our forests? The production of the forests of the province of New Brunswick is as good as that of any other part of Canada. Our forests are our greatest asset. Most hon. members know that in New Brunswick our spruce trees grow faster than they do in any other part of the world. As I say, it is our greatest asset in New Brunswick. What has happened? Besides the many pulp mills which we already have in New Brunswick there is another pulp mill being built at the present time. There are other people who are interested in pulp mills who are making inquiries with the hope and the intention of building pulp mills in New Brunswick. Why are they coming? They are coming because we have this great raw material; and, second, because we now have electric power which will help them in their operations.
I will not go into the fishing industry to any great extent. My constituency is not a fishing constituency, but I think it is generally understood that the fisheries of the maritime provinces today are in as good a condition as the fisheries of any other part of Canada. As a matter of fact, speaking of the assistance which the federal government is giving, I notice that in 1957, when the Liberal government was in power for the last time, the assistance given the fisheries in New Brunswick amounted to $697,037. Last year, 1959, the assistance given by the Department of Fisheries to the province of New Brunswick amounted to $1,102,040, a difference of over $300,000. This will indicate the great interest which is being taken by that department as far as our fishing industry is concerned.
What about agriculture? I have been in the House of Commons a good many years and I must say that with all our troubles in the maritimes I have heard fewer complaints from the maritimes or from the Atlantic provinces about agriculture than I have heard from any other part of Canada, particularly the west. I am not complaining about that, Mr. Speaker, because I know the west has a terrific problem in its great wheat crop and the matter of selling wheat is one of the biggest problems we have in Canada today or we have had in Canada for a number of years. But we get very few complaints from the agriculturists or the farmers in the maritime provinces. I had letters the other day


thanking this government-and thanking me -for the assistance which has been given to the dairy industry in Canada. I have the largest dairy centre in the maritime provinces; I have two large butter factories and my whole constituency is made up mostly of dairy farmers. They are satisfied and pleased with what is being done and has been done by the Department of Agriculture in Ottawa.
If I may I should like to mention some other assistance which has been of great benefit to our province and to the three other Atlantic provinces. I refer to the roads to resources. It is true that the roads to resources program touches every province in Canada except Quebec. The sum of $15 million is to be spent in each province, half by the province and half by the federal government; but I wish to point out that the little province of Prince Edward Island gets the same amount as the province of Ontario. The small province of New Brunswick gets the same amount, namely $7,500,000, as does the province of British Columbia; that is, we are used exactly in the same way.
Hon. members can imagine what $7,500,000 can do in building roads in Prince Edward Island; they can also realize how little it will do for the great province of Ontario. But I wish to point this out. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) informs me that not one province in Canada except Saskatchewan complained about the smaller maritime provinces being given what might be termed a great advantage in the building of roads to resources compared with larger provinces.
This is a great help to the four Atlantic provinces, particularly to the province of Newfoundland. I happened to be in Newfoundland in 1958 and, as a matter of fact, had been there a number of times. But what has struck me on each visit is how few roads there are in that great province. It has also occurred to me that if the Liberal government, for which party the province of Newfoundland has so much love, had made contributions to Newfoundland when it was in power on anything like the same scale as the present government has in the last three years the road situation in Newfoundland would have been infinitely better.
The federal government has made adjustment grants, for instance, to the four Atlantic provinces amounting to $7,500,000 a year. If the province of Newfoundland had received the same attention from the Liberal government over the 10 years from 1948 to 1958, if that province had received $7,500,000 a year it would have had $75 million to spend on roads and Newfoundland would have had roads instead of horse tracks in many parts of that province.

Let us take the question of public works. Let us take a trip through the province of New Brunswick, as I have done on many occasions. We will start with the northern part of our province. Shortly after this government came into power it authorized the building of a bridge between Campbellton, New Brunswick, and Cross Point in the province of Quebec. My mind goes back 10 or 12 years even longer to the time when former Premier McNair of the province of New Brunswick requested that a bridge be built between these two points. He put up a very strong and just argument but his argument fell on deaf ears. Nothing was done until the Conservative government came into power in 1957 when it was decided that we would give our share of the over $3 million required to build this bridge between Quebec and New Brunswick.
Go to Dalhousie and look at the work we have done in the harbour there. Go to Bathurst in the constituency of the hon. member for Gloucester. Nothing was done about the harbour there for years. The present government has made plans to dredge the harbour and make it a really good harbour. One can go anywhere in the province of New Brunswick and one will find that where the fishermen are concerned the government has been building wharves and breakwaters and assisting the fishermen and others along the coast of New Brunswick in every way.
Then we have Campobello island. For years this island with a population of over 1,200 people has had practically no access to the mainland. The Liberal government was asked for assistance and no assistance was given. At the present time arrangements are being made to build a bridge from Campobello island to Lubec in the state of Maine. Part of the cost is to be paid by the federal government, part by the province of New Brunswick and part by the state of Maine.
I could mention many other undertakings such as the numerous public buildings in the cities and towns which have been built in the very short time that the present government has been in power. Never in the history of the Atlantic provinces, particularly the province of New Brunswick, has so much been done as has been done in the last three years since the Diefenbaker government came into power.
Let us mention finance. When one speaks of giving assistance to the provinces one begins to think of money. Of course, money is the best form of assistance that can be given to any province or any people if you wish to assist them in a practical way. I have mentioned what this government has given. We

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces have given $100 million by way of adjustment grants to be paid to the Atlantic provinces over four years at the rate of $25 million a year. That is $25 million a year over and above what is received by any other province in Canada.
I have mentioned roads to resources and I want to point out the effect this has had on the economy and the budgeting of my province. I remember that for years we were continually going into debt. This year the province of New Brunswick declared a substantial surplus. The province could never have had a surplus if it had not been for the money it received from the federal treasury. In 1957, the last year the Liberal government was in power, the provincial government of New Brunswick received $19,967,729 in unconditional grants but in 1959 the figure was $32,638,620. Surely that tells a story not only to the people of the province of New Brunswick but to all the people of Canada.
When the hon. member for Gloucester spoke yesterday he said that the increase was due to the increase in population. The increase is about $13 million, an increase of more than 33J per cent. Surely no one with common sense would attribute that to an increase in population. It is due to the generosity and desire of the present government to help the province of New Brunswick and the other Atlantic provinces. Since 1952 the net debt of the province has been reduced from $218 per capita to $180 per capita in 1959, the lowest figure in many years. Of course, all these things have been possible because, in addition to receiving assistance from the federal government, we have had a very able government in the province of New Brunswick.
In closing may I repeat that there is no question that we in the Atlantic area have our problems that have not been solved. In the short time it has been in power the present government has done everything in its power to help solve these problems. What is true as to problems in the maritimes is of course also true as to problems in other parts of Canada. The expansion of the Canadian economy this year has been on a vast scale. All parts of Canada have not shared in it equally, but all have shared in it. I have faith that the Atlantic area will grow in economic strength with the rest of Canada. I do not take any pessimistic view, and I believe the future of these regions is a good one. No one who knows its people and areas as I do can entertain any doubts as to the future of the Atlantic provinces.
As I have already said, it has been a recognized aim of federal policy to provide fiscal aid to the Atlantic area. The dominion government is continuing, in many ways, to

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces assist the people of our four provinces to win for themselves a prosperous and secure future.

speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the minister, but his time has expired.
I just have one more sentence.
Go ahead.

I was saying, just in closing, that for years past the economy and prosperity of the Atlantic provinces had not been in any way comparable to the other provinces of Canada. I believe today we are approaching nearer to it than we ever were before. If I may cut my conclusion real short, Mr. Speaker, then it is needless for me to say it is my intention to vote against the amendment and the subamendment. Yesterday the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) said that it was a vote of non-confidence in the government, and that is exactly what it is. We, in the Atlantic provinces, have confidence in this government. We have every reason to have confidence in it, and we will show our confidence by voting and giving it our support whenever we can.

I feel that the debate that took place yesterday and is taking place today is a very important debate, and a very essential debate in the House of Commons. I was pleased that the official opposition, who have the right under our rules to decide the type of amendment that will be moved as a want of confidence motion, did not yield to the temptation of bringing in a motion on the Bomarc but rather took advantage of this opportunity to introduce a substantial motion that affects a large section of the Canadian nation. If they had introduced a motion on the Bomarc it would have been merely to shoot what is already a dead duck and to attempt to bury, perhaps a few weeks in advance, a weapon which I hope will be given a respectable burial within a short time.
I have not very often spoken on maritime matters, Mr. Speaker, but I have often spoken on grievances affecting a larger part of Canada. Those of us who come from western Canada have felt at times in the past that we have had particular grievances that should be raised. We think so today. We have received some attention from time to time from previous governments, and I think one of the reasons the prairies have received attention from previous governments is that we have had some extended, and sometimes spirited, debates in the House of Commons. The maritime provinces, in my opinion, have a very real grievance. The people of the maritime provinces have failed to share in Canada's prosperity from time to time. Although they

came into confederation with a relatively industrialized area, the fortunes of confederation have not been kind to the maritime provinces. I think a debate such as this will be of some benefit in pointing up their real and important problems.
From time to time we hear a good deal about basic human rights and fundamental freedoms. They usually have to do with political rights. They usually have to do with freedom of speech or equality because of race or equality before the law. But I think there is another equality to which the people in a sovereign democracy have a right, and that is their fair share in the resources and in the production of the nation of which they are a part. If that is so, as I believe it is, then the maritime provinces and the people of those provinces have a just grievance against the rest of Canada.
Of course, this is not a situation that developed in 1960. This is not a situation that developed in 22 years of Liberal government which did not give attention to this problem. This is a problem that has been developing for generations. The question today is not so much who is to blame as what is going to be done about this grave problem. Those of us in the C.C.F. movement feel that a planned economy, that an extension of government responsibility and government control, that a vast expansion of directed public funds in regional investment, are absolutely essential. We are certain that if the present economic system is allowed to go uncontrolled, undirected, whether this is done with a Conservative government in power or a Liberal government in power will make no difference whatever but will continue to relegate the people of the mari-times to a position of economic second-class citizens.
We have heard a lot from government members about the situation. If one were to listen to them he would think there was no problem at all, that everything had been solved, that all you had to have was three years of Tory administration and the worries of the maritime provinces had come to an end. The shorter of the members for Halifax [DOT]-I understand they do not like to be referred to as the senior or junior member-last evening talked about the Atlantic resolutions. He said the resolutions were and are, and will remain, a beacon of light after 20 years of darkness for the people of the Atlantic provinces. It is not a beacon of light the people want; it is not more talk about a vision; it is not some pie in the sky. They want jobs now. They want the government to implement the Atlantic resolutions instead of talking about a beacon of light.

The hon. member went on to say, after giving some economic forecasts about capital and repair expenditures, that we have here the highest capital intentions of any year in Nova Scotia's history. The people of Nova Scotia have been living on intentions for years, good intentions. 1 do not believe it helps them much that the intentions now come from a Tory government rather than from a Liberal government.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) made a very interesting speech and, since he is an old friend of mine of many years' standing in the House of Commons, I listened to him with great attention and great respect. However, I detected all through his speech a note of self-satisfaction that all was well. The maritimes had turned the corner and, under a Conservative administration, at long last they were coming into their own. He did not give us the unemployment statistics. He did not tell us why there are more unemployed in the maritimes now than there have been for some years. He did not tell us why the total number of persons in the maritimes with jobs is 449,000, and yet the registrations at the national employment service office total 116,488.
There is widespread and serious unemployment in the maritime provinces about which this government is doing absolutely nothing. The same report shows that in the province of Ontario there are 2,192,000 persons with jobs and 240,668 registrations at the national employment service offices. In Ontario 9.1 persons had jobs for every person registered at the national employment service offices; in the maritimes only 3.85 persons had jobs for every person registered at the national employment service offices. Unemployment in the maritimes is more than twice as serious as in Ontario. If we could take care of the people of the maritimes with nice pious statements and a lot of soothing syrup then they should be well satisfied after listening to members of the government.
Hon. members opposite have not been frank enough to tell us that the problem in the maritimes is still exceedingly serious, that the unemployment situation has deteriorated rather than improved and that relative incomes of people of the maritimes compared with those of other Canadians are disgracefully low.
I have in my hand a portion of the Gordon royal commission report entitled, "Some Regional Aspects of Canada's Economic Development". In table 9 on page 45 the per capita income for the years 1951-55 is shown for the various provinces. I will mention only the incomes of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as related to the per capita income
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces of Ontario, the province with the highest income. The government has been saying that conditions in the maritimes are improving and that the people there are better off than they were in the past. Conditions were not good back in 1951-55. The per capita income in New Brunswick was $787 compared with a per capita income of $1,448 in Ontario. I have done some arithmetic on this, comparing these figures with the latest figures for per capita income in the provinces in 1958. The per capita income in 1958 in New Brunswick was $919 and in Ontario it was $1,696. How much better off are the people of New Brunswick with respect to income and cash dollars about which the Minister of Veterans Affairs spoke so eloquently?
In 1951-55, according to the report of the Gordon commission, the per capita income in New Brunswick was some 54 per cent of the per capita income in Ontario and under this wonderful Conservative administration about which we have heard so much and after having done such a fine job the people are in exactly the position they were in under the previous administration. Per capita income in New Brunswick is still just 54 per cent of the per capita income in Ontario. Where is the improvement? Where is the great development in the maritimes that has resulted from the Conservative administration? The percentage of per capita income is just as low under the Tories as it was under the Liberals.
What about Nova Scotia? In 1951-55 according to the report Nova Scotia had a per capita income of $880 as compared with $1,448 in Ontario. According to my calculations this works out at 63 per cent. The latest statistics available for 1958 show that the per capita income in Nova Scotia had risen to $1,072 compared with $1,696 in Ontario, still 63 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? Is the per capita income per person in the whole population of these provinces or per the working force?
The whole population, I take it.
That makes a difference.

My hon. friend may want to look at family statistics and I would appreciate his talking about them but it does not make any difference. I do not think that families under the Conservatives are bigger than they were under the Liberals. My point is that the per capita income in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as compared with the per capita income in Ontario, the province with the highest income, is just as low

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces under the Tories as it was under the Liberals, yet because the Conservative government is in power they are complacent and say, "All is well; we are doing a fine job". The only recommendation is that the conditions are no worse than they were under the previous administration.

Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? Do I understand that while he has pointed out that there has been a substantial increase in per capita income in the maritimes he seems to think this is of no avail whatever because there has also been an increase in Ontario and the percentage of difference is still the same? Now, granted, we would all be pleased if the income in New Brunswick had risen so much more that it had overtaken Ontario, but does the hon. member suggest that that very substantial increase which has taken place is not of great avail in New Brunswick?
That is not what we have heard from hon. gentlemen opposite. I am of course glad to see any increase in the per capita income in any part of Canada.
Well, hurray.
How are you getting along in Saskatchewan?
I just wish that the Tories were glad of this too instead of bringing in balanced budgets that are balanced on the backs of half a million unemployed or perhaps more.
Oh, oh.
How are you getting along out in Saskatchewan? The hon. gentleman will not answer.

The great grievance of the maritimes has been that they have not shared in a proportionate way in the production of the Canadian nation. This grievance remains the same now and in the same proportion as it was under the previous administration. I am convinced that if you allow the present uncontrolled monopolistic dog eat dog system to go unchecked as is the wish of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) the people of the maritimes will continue to be second-class citizens as far as economic standards are concerned. We suggest the time has come for government action. My hon. friends in the Liberal party can beat their breasts about how much they believe in free enterprise but the proof of the pudding is in the eating and free enterprise is in disgrace in this country because it is failing the people of the maritimes, the unemployed and hundreds of other Canadians.
[Mr. Argue.)
What about Saskatchewan?

There is one voice on the government side of the house that has expressed some realization of the difficulties being faced in the maritimes. On February 26 as reported at page 1489 of Hansard this statement was made:
The economic problems in Restigouche-Mada-waska and in the maritime provinces generally were always bad, but when you come along with a policy of tight money conditions become a hundred times worse.
There is a statement from a Conservative member in good standing in the Conservative party who says to the government that things were bad under the Liberals but that now with Tory tight money conditions are one hundred times worse. Mr. Speaker, political recrimination will not help the people of the maritime provinces.
I am glad this motion has been brought forward. I am exceedingly disappointed by the answers of members of the government, because their answers today to the desires of the maritime provinces are one big "No". They do not intend to do any more in the future than they have done in the past, even though the record is that conditions in the maritimes now are as bad, if not worse, as they were under the administration of the former Liberal government.
Mr. Speaker, we think that the time has come for government action and for public funds to be directed into the development of the Atlantic provinces. We suggest that Canadian citizens living in the maritime provinces have a right to share equitably in the production of this country. I would suggest that the government should offer a portfolio to enable members to discover what the duties of the minister are, because we imagine he could handle his portfolio during the normal coffee break, shall we say, in the morning. They might take one of the interested cabinet ministers and make him a minister of a new department, a department of regional and economic development, a department whose specific purpose would be to see that regionally depressed areas such as the maritime provinces, Elliot Lake, Uranium City in Saskatchewan and other areas of the country receive attention from the national government. This calls for money, and here I agree with the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I suggest there should be a capital development budget of at least $1 billion of public funds for development of the economy of depressed areas.
If there are interruptions that this is too much, it is just 3 per cent of the gross national product; it is just 16 per cent of the amount now being spent by way of our

national budget; and it is just over 60 per cent of the money now being spent and largely wasted on national defence.
I would suggest that monies can be obtained for a great capital development program; that as it becomes necessary to reduce our defence expenditures the people of the maritime provinces should not be forced to suffer even more but that some large part of these savings should go into the regional development fund. I would suggest that the government should give speedy attention to such things as the Chignecto canal which holds real promise. I would suggest that the government should say what it intends to do about a causeway to Prince Edward Island. I would suggest that the government should take action to help the export industries of the maritime provinces, as well as other exporting industries in Canada such as the forestry industry and the fishing industry, by instituting a system of economic policies which will bring the Canadian dollar into par with the United States dollar and thus bolster Canada's export industry. I think it is national madness for our country to follow a policy which cripples our export industries and puts the nation in hock to foreign investors which this past year amounts to almost $1.5 billion.
I would suggest that there are other great programs for economic development. There should be a start made on an over-all highway program for Canada. The government should not be satisfied with the one highway ribbon that it is helping to promote across our country. I would suggest that for the maritime provinces as for the rest of Canada there should be a great housing development instead of the Tory policy of cutting housing, allowing the slums to remain and failing to take care of the housing needs of Canadians.
I am convinced that at this time more and more people in the maritime provinces are questioning the very tenets of the policies both of the Conservative government and the Liberal party. I hear very interesting and encouraging reports of the support that is coming to the C.C.F. party particularly in the province of Nova Scotia. This debate is bringing the attention of parliament to the needs of the maritime provinces.
There are other ways whereby people can bring to the attention of the government and the Canadian nation their needs. It can be done in provincial elections about which this government was so satisfied when provincial Liberal governments were overturned, and we used to hear so much of that in the house. Action can be taken on a provincial basis and other action can be taken.

I make no apology for the delegation which came from the prairie provinces a year ago to impress upon this government and the Canadian nation in a very vivid way conditions in the prairie provinces which condemned citizens in those areas of our agricultural industry to an inferior position. I think the people of the maritime provinces who have a just cause would be well advised to consider sending large delegations to wait on the government, which is their democratic right, in order to bring to the Canadian nation in a vivid and spectacular way the very important, serious and just grievances which are theirs. Delegations are an excellent method of focusing attention on problems in a democratic country.
Mr. Speaker, in the final analysis the only real solution will come by a very definite, decided and drastic change in the principles operating in our economic society.
