speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the opportunity to speak on this motion today. I tried to recall the different points made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) in opening the debate yesterday. I am not quite sure that he was serious in what he was saying, but he gave me the impression, as I think he must have given others, that he had no great heart in the task he was undertaking.
He selected the Atlantic provinces as the area in which he attempted to show that the Conservative government had failed to carry out its promises which they made before the election of 1957. At this time he took the opportunity to consider our record because of the impending elections in the two provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick which will be held within the next month or so. So he concentrated on that topic, the elections being over in Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island.
Of course, there was not much he could say about Prince Edward Island. He had no complaint about that province because the people themselves had given their verdict in the general election which took place last year and had overturned a Liberal government that had been in office, I think, for over 20 years.
With regard to Newfoundland, I am sure he must have been aware of what the premier of that province said recently. He is quoted as saying that anybody would be foolish to blame the government in Ottawa for the recent recession.
However, the hon. member did manage once more to accuse this government of repudiating the constitution in regard to term 29. I have heard the hon. member say that

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces before, and I resent that statement. The h<jn. member knows perfectly well that the constitution has not been repudiated, and that we have carried out the recommendation of the McNair commission We are carrying out that recommendation, and we have provided for a review as was asked for by counsel for the Newfoundland government and by the premier of that government. We are having that review take place before 1962, not three years later as the premier wanted.
He produced then some of the resolutions which were passed by a group of candidates who met in Moncton before the election of 1957, the resolutions which the hon. member called the Atlantic charter. It is important to remember what the circumstances of that meeting were. At that time the hon. member had, I believe, become a member of the government and we were then in opposition. The Progressive Conservative candidates met in Moncton and, actuated by the knowledge that the Atlantic provinces had been neglected for a long period, we considered what methods could best be adopted in order to bring about an improvement. Thus, we set out the objectives at which we should aim.
The complaint of the hon. member and his associates is that we have not attained all these objectives at the present time. Bearing in mind the economic difficulties of the maritime provinces-and these have been set out today by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter)-it is not surprising that we have not been able to carry out all our intentions in the short space of three years. I think it is something of which we can be proud that we have been able to do as much as we have. We do not pretend to have solved all the problems; we do not pretend to have all the answers. On the other hand, we are doing all we can, and we have done all we can; we intend to give attention to all these problems as they are brought before us in the proper way.
The mover of this amendment then gave a brief general review under various headings: industry, coal, agriculture, fisheries, roads, transportation, the tourist industry, mining and finance. I do not think he mentioned power, which constituted such an important feature of the contribution made by the Conservative government to the expansion and development which has been taking place in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick during the past three years. I propose, myself, to say a few words about the subjects with which the hon. member dealt, but before I embark on that undertaking I should like to say something which I believe must be obvious to everyone here, namely that the
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West).}

federal government is not responsible for everything which takes place or which does not take place in the Atlantic provinces or any of the other provinces; we cannot interfere in the affairs of the provincial governments even to the slightest degree.
The provinces are autonomous and selfgoverning with regard to everything which is within their own jurisdiction. Nobody should know that better than the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, because in Newfoundland we have the sole Liberal government in Canada today. Surely he does not expect the federal Conservative government to be responsible for the sins and omissions of that government. Neither can the federal government take credit-and we do not take credit- for what is being done of a beneficial nature in the provinces. I recommend to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) that he read the speech made by the president of the Atlantic provinces economic council contained in the April edition of the Atlantic Advocate. Mr. Arthur Johnson, the president, is the deputy minister of the economic development department, of which Premier Smallwood is the minister in charge. If the hon. member for Gloucester would read that speech I think he would finish up by holding a view different from the one he expressed yesterday. To get the drift of his remarks, I now propose to quote from page 3483 of Hansard what the hon. member said:
We are not asking for hand-outs. The central provinces and the western provinces know what we of the Atlantic provinces need. Just a week ago I was visiting one of my constituents and X noticed that the car at his door was manufactured in Ontario.

Just imagine the hon. member getting down to look at the door knob to see where it was made.

The furniture came from Quebec.

When I went into the kitchen I saw that the washing machine, the refrigerator, the toaster and everything were manufactured in Quebec and Ontario.

I draw the attention of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who prides himself on being a free trader, to the attitude of the hon. member for Gloucester.

The former Liberal government was aware in 1956, as the secret report informed us, that there was to be a recession, and it did come to a head in 1957. He pointed out the Liberal government in 1956 had made concessions to the people all over Canada, in all the provinces, of about $106 million, and that the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island had benefited by about $9 million a year.
Then, the hon. member made reference to the question of agriculture, and he referred to agriculture in his own riding. I do not


have much knowledge of the small settlements in his riding where agriculture assumes some local importance, but I think he will admit that if agriculture declined in Newfoundland it has been due particularly to the impact of confederation, bearing in mind that the former Liberal government at Ottawa subsidized a vessel, jointly with the government of Prince Edward Island, for the shipping of agricultural produce to Newfoundland. I think he will agree that it was very difficult for the farmers of Newfoundland to carry on their industry after confederation.
Will the minister permit a question?
No.
The industry is at its lowest ebb today.
Would the minister say a subsidy is not being given by the present government to a vessel for the precise purpose that he mentioned?

Yes, but it was started by the Liberal government. The Liberal government likes to take credit for the things it started, so we will give it credit now. It is being partly paid by the Conservative government of Prince Edward Island at the present time but that, too, was started by a Liberal government.
However, there are some important farms in Newfoundland. I would draw the attention of hon. members to the great farm that is owned by the premier of Newfoundland on Roche's line. I would like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to tell us something about it, because I believe he had the privilege of spending a night there as the guest of the distinguished squire who presides over that magnificent farm. It is supposed to have the greatest number of cattle on any farm in eastern Canada, and I think the number of chickens there-some of them have come home to roost-goes into the many thousands.
They come home to roost every night, you know.

They will come home to roost eventually for the premier of Newfoundland.
I do not know why the hon. member referred to farming because I have always been under the impression that farming has been successfully practised in the maritime provinces. They have large areas of fine agricultural land, and the produce from Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is famous. We in Newfoundland, of

course, have been accustomed all our lives to buying produce from those places. I know they come on the market here as well.
Then he referred to fisheries and he regretted the preponderance of our fish finding its way to the United States market as fresh frozen fish.
1 am sure the hon. gentleman-

He did not
say it in so many words.
I certainly do not regret it; I regret we do not sell more there.
The hon. member spoke about the large quantities of fresh fish exported to the markets as if it was something to be regretted.
I did not speak that way.

He knows that during the past 40 years, since the first world war, the countries of Europe which used to purchase large quantities of our salt fish have gone into building fleets of their own and catching their own fish. Spain, Portugal and Italy particularly send out large fleets every year to the Grand Banks and catch their own fish and salt and cure it for their people.
The policy of the Newfoundland government in regard to fisheries was to finance the building of large fresh fish plants and the fresh fish plant operators were able to borrow the money from the government of Newfoundland, as high as $5 million, to help them establish those industries, so that great financial assistance given by the government of Newfoundland resulted in an incentive to the production of fresh fish.
Then, again, the recruiting for United States bases construction of large numbers of our people who live along the long extended coast line of thousands of miles around the island took place. They were drawn away from the fishery and went to work as labourers, carpenters and carpenters' helpers, and at other work. It was the policy of the government to take 10,000 men out of the fishing boats. Their fishing gear went to ruin, and not so many of them are engaged in fishing today as formerly. Those who are engaged in it are engaged mostly in catching fresh fish which they sell to the fresh fish plants; or partly making fish which they sell at times to fish buyers who come to Newfoundland from Nova Scotia. But our government at Ottawa has also given assistance to the fisheries. The hon. member knew about that but he did not say anything about it. Last year
3, 1960
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces we built 20 community stages in Newfoundland and a good many of them were in the hon. gentleman's own riding.
Over half of them.

He did not
make any reference to the assistance given to the fisheries by the government. We have reorganized the bait services. I do not think our fishermen will be able to complain of a shortage of bait as they were able to in the past. Anybody who knows anything about the Newfoundland fisheries knows how important is the question of bait supply. The federal government has gone out of its way to implement the report of the Newfoundland royal commission on the fisheries of the southwest coast. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo must be aware of the several expensive wharves that have been built or are being built to assist the Newfoundland government solve the problem of the fishermen of the southwest coast.
Again, we have built a new ferry for service between Portugal Cove and Bell island. We have built two new icebreakers and new government steamers. The St. John's harbour development, which was one of those projects thought about by the former Liberal government and put on the shelf, is being carried out by the present Conservative government. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate complimented his colleague, the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Granger), on the speech he made recently regarding the fisheries of Labrador. But if I am right I think the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador was advocating a return to the Labrador fishery. He can correct me if I am wrong but I think that is what he recommended. I should like to draw to his attention the fact that in 1951 a former minister of fisheries, Mr. Mayhew, put the kibosh on the Labrador fishery when he said that no further support would be given under the Fisheries Prices Support Act to fishermen fishing on the Labrador. There is not much use in anybody going in for that unless that decision is changed and I do not think the fishermen of Newfoundland have gone to Labrador to anything like the same extent since that was done.
The mover of the amendment did have a good word to say about the pulp and paper industry, especially in Newfoundland where it is booming. I do not know whether he made any reference to the new pulp mill being built in Nova Scotia which will cost $45 million. That has always been regarded in Newfoundland as the high water mark of government accomplishment. It will mean a great boon to that part of Nova Scotia where the mill is going to be built.

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces
On the subject of mining the hon. member acknowledged the remarkable expansion and development taking place at Carol lake and to take place before long, I hope, at lake Wabush. This Labrador-Quebec mineralized area is in for a tremendous boom and the results of the expansion in employment will be felt in many other parts of Canada as well.
With regard to transportation, a problem that has agitated the business people in the Atlantic provinces and the federal government as well as the governments of the maritime provinces, we have appointed a royal commission which is now investigating the transportation problems of all parts of Canada and more particularly those of the Atlantic provinces. I hope that the commission will be able to bring in a report which we can implement and which will be of benefit to business people and people generally in these provinces.
My colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, referred to the subject of coal, a subject to which the hon. member for Gloucester has constantly referred. Notwithstanding the sweeping expansion of oil and gas distribution in the last few years which has been phenomenal-I do not know whether people realize how much domestic consumers have taken to using gas and oil-and the decline in consumption of coal by 50 per cent, the amount of coal mined in Nova Scotia last year increased over the previous year. We have given annual subventions to the coal industry of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick since we have been in office. Last year we gave nearly $14 million and in the estimates this year there is provision for the same amount. I wish the hon. member for Gloucester would get out his pencil, write down all these figures, add them up and see if they are not an indication of the interest that the government has taken in the welfare of the people of the maritime provinces.
Production is still going down.

I should like to refer to the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) and point out to him that the steel industry of Nova Scotia is one of the oldest industries in Canada. We in Newfoundland have a particular interest in the Nova Scotia steel industry. Many of our people work there. I suppose there are as many people from Newfoundland in Sydney and Glace Bay as there are from any other part of Canada. We supply the iron ore that is used in the manufacture of steel. We supply the limestone from Aguathuna in the Port au Port region of Newfoundland in the constituency of Humber-St. George's. We make a

tremendous contribution to the manufacture of steel in Nova Scotia and therefore we are vitally interested in seing the steel industry of Nova Scotia retain and, if possible, increase its importance.
But the hon. member must know, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) knows, that there has been a rapid expansion in the steel industry, notably at Sault Ste. Marie and Hamilton. Only this morning there was an item in the paper that the premier of Quebec had attended a ceremony yesterday to mark the coming into existence of a new mill for making steel pipe. The fact that there is such tremendous production of iron ore in the province of Quebec and also in the Labrador part of the province of Newfoundland and such cheap transportation from Seven Islands to the area below Montreal makes me believe quite strongly that a big steel industry is going to come into being in the province of Quebec. I believe that the prediction made by the premier of Quebec is going to be fulfilled.

It is coming to fruition now and I am sure the hon. member must wish it as much as I do.

speechtext: I have been saying it was coming for years.

Despite the undoubted and tremendous progress in the steel industry, which was given great impetus last year because of the strike in the steel mills of the United States, we cannot possibly manufacture all the iron ore that we produce. We just cannot do it. Next year we will probably be producing 20 to 30 million tons in the Labrador-Quebec area alone. Then we have Bell island and Steep Rock and there are other mines coming into production in different parts of Canada. We must export ore. We should be grateful that we have near us in the New York-Pittsburgh area great steel mills that can take all the ore we can produce. This will mean employment for the miners and for those in the service enterprises who supply the workers, for the railways and the steamers that operate to bring the ore to this great steel market in the United States.
I find that all the C.C.F. members are nothing if not generous with money. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said that his program would cost $500 million. His leader

doubled that and made it $1 billion. I say to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, where would he get the $500 million in the first place and what would he do with it when he got it? He did not elaborate on that at all. He gets up, and his leader does the same, and with this offhand generosity distributes this money.
We have been criticized and badgered because of our few-no, I will not say few, I will say something else-because we had a deficit this year of $400 million. Last year, we had a bigger deficit. We are badgered, we are criticized and told we are not running things right. If we do not have a deficit, we have to increase taxes. This government could increase taxes and get the money to pay for these things. Who is in favour of increasing taxes?
The C.C.F.

Yes, so long as they increase the taxes for somebody else. They have no interest in business. They are not in favour of private business at all. I do not want to get into that subject at all, but all they have to do is look at the United States, the richest country in the world, and think that the people achieved their tremendous prosperity through private enterprise. How they can seriously stand up for state ownership is more than I can understand. You can only have successful state ownership when you have communism as you have in Russia and the countries behind the iron curtain. The sooner those hon. members realize that-perhaps they do realize it-the better. He spoke about $500 million as a modest beginning. I suppose his leader has gone a step further and made it $1 billion, and if any other hon. members speak the whole revenue will be gone out in that sort of thing.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had a good word to say about the financial assistance that we provided in 1958 for the Atlantic provinces. The hon. member for Gloucester and the hon. member for Northum-berland-Miramichi (Mr. McWilliam) even damned it with faint praise. Well, they could not say anything else. This $7.5 million which is going to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland and the $2.5 million for Prince Edward Island, making a total of $25 million, will be paid for four years. This will amount to $100 million in four years. These payments have been of tremendous importance to these provinces. We can hardly begin to think of all the benefits that have come to those provinces, in which there are only one and one-third million people, from the expenditure of $25 million a year.
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces
Let me point this out-I do not know whether it is discouraging to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-several times the hon. member referred to the desirability of finishing the trans-Canada highway, especially in Newfoundland. His party had a program whereby the Liberals, if they had been elected, would build the trans-Canada highway. Let me point this out-
That is not right; we would pay 90 per cent of the cost.

Ninety per cent of the cost. I am going to show the hon. member how the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland could have been built twice over if the government of that province had been really a sensible government. In the first place, they put $30 million into secondary industries, with the help of German industrialists, most of which went down the drain and from which not one cent ever came back. After all, if $30 million had been spent on the trans-Canada highway, the trans-Canada highway would be an accomplished fact now.
Then, if the government of Newfoundland took the $7.5 million we have been giving them for the past two years, and will give them for the next two years, and spent that on the trans-Canada highway, we would have a trans-Canada highway by 1962. Then we would be able to talk about a tourist industry. The tourists do not want to go to a place where the roads are dusty when it is dry and muddy when it is wet. The tourists want to drive on good roads; that is the first essential for a tourist industry. This would have been a sensible and sound undertaking, and would have brought thousands of tourists to the province of Newfoundland. After all, this year in Newfoundland, this very month, we are celebrating the 350th anniversary of the first colony of the British empire. Three hundred and fifty years ago John Guy, an alderman from Bristol, came out to Newfoundland and made a settlement at Cupids. There was, thus, the first British colony at Conception bay 350 years ago.
This would have been a great time to have our trans-Canada highway. We have other places of historic interest such as cape Bonavista, the first place seen by John Cabot, and Placentia, where the French priests and the French soldiers lived at one time, as well as Ferryland. Both these latter places are in my own constituency. Newfoundland is a most interesting, and certainly the oldest part of Canada. Thousands of tourists, not only from Newfoundland but from the United States would be happy to visit Newfoundland if the trans-Canada highway were built.
I should like to speak of the assistance we have given to the Atlantic provinces for the
3516	HOUSE OF
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces construction and improvement of their power projects. The previous government also dil-lied and dallied with this idea and did nothing about it. As the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) explained this afternoon-
That is not correct.

Oh, they sent Mr. Howe down to officiate at the opening, but they gave no financial assistance to the Beechwood project. We lent them money to pay off debts at the bank that the government had incurred. We provided $13 million in the last three years for subventions on coal, partly used for the production of electricity. We have provided over $10 million for the building of steam power plants and the erection of transmission lines in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I do not know how many members are aware of this, but we made an offer to Newfoundland to build transmission lines from Bay d'Espoir to Grand Falls at a cost of $11 million and give the Newfoundland government 40 years in which to pay off this substantial loan. So, I think we have provided innumerable benefits to the Atlantic provinces.
People like my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo seem to think there is something improper or indecent in talking about what the government has done to assist these provinces. When we are challenged like this there is nothing else for us to do except point out the things we have done. I have here a report of the power commission of New Brunswick for the year ending March 31, 1959. I should like to give two or three figures from this statement of their operations for the previous year. This statement shows that the kilowatt capacity at March 31, 1957 was 132,575 kilowatts; at the end of March, 1959, it had risen to 204,525, that is an increase of over 55 per cent. The total generation of kilowatts had increased from 606 million to 754 million, an increase of 25 per cent. The total energy distributed increased from 534 million to 676 million. There was a substantial increase in the sale of electrical energy in the province of New Brunswick. In a time of depression, that could not happen. The number of retail customers increased from 75,316 at the end of March, 1957 to 82,655, an increase of 7,300 in two years.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate on the problems of the Atlantic provinces I feel an especial pleasure in following my friend the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Browne) because, among other things, it gives me an opportunity to wish him well and send him our congratulations on his birthday. I do so with the greater pleasure because he is exactly ten days younger than I am and I hope that I look and act as youthful and vigorous as he does.
Mr. Speaker, we have been discussing this problem in a way which I think makes it quite clear, whatever side of the house we are on, that there is with us now and indeed there has been for a long time the problem of economic underdevelopment in this part of our country. The problem of the development of new areas, Arctic areas and others if you like, is an important one and we all want to see that proceeded with. But it is of equal if not of greater importance that we should redevelop those areas of Canada whose people have in the past contributed so much to our country but who have through no fault of their own been forced to lag behind in the march of national progress, perhaps so far as material things are concerned.
This need for redevelopment is great. It is a most urgent problem of public policy. There has been progress made in this respect in the last few decades but in spite of that progress average incomes in those parts of Canada are still well behind those in the rest of Canada. A wide and persistent gap remains and as long as it does remain it constitutes a strain, as it is bound to, on the kind of complete national unity we want. As long as it remains there is bound to be a regional problem.
The rate of economic progress in the three maritime provinces between 1926 and 1955- and I quote the figures of the Gordon commission on this point-show that personal income in constant dollars during that period -and it is a considerable period-increased by 94 per cent while in the six other provinces it increased by only 80 per cent. In other words the rate of increase was greater in the maritimes during those years but nevertheless in 1955 in that part of Canada personal income was 37 per cent below that

in the rest of the country and the average family income was 31 per cent below the rest of the country. Therefore a faster rate of growth is essential in the Atlantic provinces if the gap to which I referred is going to be closed and if those provinces are going to catch up with the rest of the country in economic and material development.
From 1956 to 1958 the figures show that that gap is not being closed. The per capita income in 1958 again in constant dollars was up, I will admit, in Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia but it was down in New Brunswick. The average income in 1958 as compared with the Canadian average as a whole was below the national average by $482. That is the average income in the Atlantic provinces compared with the average income in the country as a whole.
Although there has been some improvement over recent years there has not been enough improvement and the improvement such as it has been is largely due to transfer payments from the federal government; as has already been pointed out in this discussion. These payments account for nearly one quarter of the increase in personal per capita income in the maritime provinces since 1926. Indeed, in 1958, the last year for which I have figures, the transfer payments to the Atlantic provinces made up 16.3 per cent of the total personal income in the Atlantic area. Total personal income amounted in that year to $1,731 million of which $283 million came from transfer payments from the federal government.
These payments are useful and indeed they are essential to the welfare of those provinces. No one regrets for a minute that they should have been received especially in the Atlantic provinces which over the years have made their own transfer payments of another kind to the rest of Canada. We are all the beneficiaries of that kind of transfer, inside this house and outside of it. While no one regrets these payments and are glad they have been made something else is required to reduce this disproportionate reliance on government transfers. That something else, of course, must be new capital investment.
In so far as that kind of capital investment is taking place in the Atlantic provinces-and there have been examples of it given in this discussion-we all rejoice but notwithstanding the remarks just made by my hon. friend it has not happened in any significant way or to a degree that has had any significant effect in closing this gap. The official figures prove that.
In 1953 the proportion of Canada's total capital outlays made in the Atlantic region
3,	1960
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces were 6.2 per cent. In 1960, the current year, investment intentions from the recent report of the department on that subject show that that figure is expected to be 6.4 per cent. That is very little increase indeed and not nearly enough to bring about the expansion which we all would like to see brought about. Indeed, there are signs that point to a weakening of industrial economy rather than an expansion such as is necessary to increase income and close the gap with the rest of Canada.
In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick between 1956 and 1959 industrial employment has decreased by 8.4 index points for New Brunswick and 5.4 index points for Nova Scotia. It is up in Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island but the base from which to advance there is a very low one indeed.
One feature that has been referred to by nearly every hon. member who has taken part in this debate and one which, notwithstanding what was said by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) last night, must cause great anxiety is the declining coal production in Nova Scotia. In 1957 the monthly average production was 474,000 tons and in 1959 it was 365,000 tons. Total production for the year through which we have just passed was 4,380,000 tons although the Minister of National Revenue put on the record the figure of 5,806,000 tons which does not correspond with any official figures we have been able to secure. It would be interesting to find out where the hon. gentleman got that figure of production because it is not the figure that appears in the federal statistics nor the one given to the Rand commission by the Nova Scotia bureau of mines. The official figures show a decrease of 23 per cent or 1.3 million tons in this two-year period.
So, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding certain hopeful signs there are indications that more will have to be done if this gap is to be filled. These signs do reflect a serious problem which we are presenting to this house in the motion before it. I suggest that development of the Atlantic region which is embodied in this motion is a main problem of public policy at this time, as it has indeed been a main subject of public pronouncements by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and members of his government.
The Prime Minister talks a great deal about development. No one quarrels with the talk providing the facts justify the talk. But I ask, is this development occurring in the Atlantic provinces at this time? Basic to this development-and I refer to what the minister who has just sat down has said-* is the situation in regard to power. On March

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces 3 over the television network the Prime Minister has this to say on this matter. I am quoting his text:
The next point-
He was talking about development.
-was a ten-year plan for the development of thermal power plants in the Atlantic provinces. This has already been provided for by legislation. The Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act has been on the statute books for two years and has resulted in immediate savings of some $20 million in power costs to the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
Mr. Speaker, that figure of $20 million saving is grossly inaccurate and therefore misleading, I shall have no difficulty in showing that by the official figures which we have received from answers made by the minister himself to questions from this side of the house.
I wish I had time to trace the origins of this very important statute, the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, which is the foundation upon which power development will have to take place in the Atlantic provinces. The proposal for a power program for the Atlantic region in the form in which it was later implemented was made on March 4, 1957 by Mr. Harris in his budget speech. As some hon. members will remember, he then made an offer which would have provided for the construction and operation of thermal plants and transmission lines by the federal government; the rental of these lines and the sale of power at cost to provincial electric systems; and the acquisition of plants and other facilities by the provinces at any time on payment of their amortized cost. That proposal, as hon. members know, grew out of a carefully conducted study by the dominion coal board through Professor Christie of John Hopkins University. Later in that session the minister of northern affairs and national resources, Mr. Lesage, made it quite clear that in carrying out this program the government of the day intended to make coal competitive with oil in the construction of these thermal plants.
Mr. Speaker, all these ideas were embodied, with one important exception, and I think in the wrong direction, in the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act which was introduced by this government and passed on, I think, January 15, 1958. So that this phase of so-called national development, the national development program, which on March 3 the Prime Minister claimed for himself and his government, was borrowed from Liberal proposals with one change, which I think was a change in the wrong direction. In piloting this bill through the House of Commons, the minister of northern affairs had this to say:


For the purposes of the two fiscal years now in contemplation,-
That is, the years 1957-58 and 1958-59.
[DOT]-a total of $12,700,000 for construction of plants and transmission lines will certainly be required.
The minister then gave the house his vision of the future power construction program right up to 1967. This must be the ten-year program the Prime Minister was talking about in his broadcast, for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Relying presumably upon estimates which were prepared for him by the Montreal Engineering Company, in this program, as he put it before this house at that time, the present minister visualized two plants for New Brunswick and eight plants for Nova Scotia at a cost of about $105 million. That statement will be found at pages 3037 and 3038 of Hansard for January 8, 1958.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us look at the realization of this particular vision. To date, for three, not for two years the money spent by the federal government on the power construction program-I get this information from Hansard from questions addressed to ministers-was $7,700,000, which is $5 million less than the minister forecast for two years. Yet the Minister of National Revenue-I am sorry he is not in his seat at the moment- said last night that $12 million had been spent already on this program. That statement appears in Hansard and I would like to know where he got that figure when his own colleague gave us a figure of $7.7 million. Of this $7.7 million, $5 million was spent on transmission lines and most of the rest on assisting the rehabilitation of the plant at Trenton in Nova Scotia.
For 1960-61, the current year, the estimates which have been laid before the house show that $4,900,000 have been appropriated for advances under this power act. That is less than last year. Yet the Minister of National Revenue said, as reported on page 3475 of Hansard, that in this current year $13 million had been pledged.
That is for subventions on coal.

With great respect, that is not what the minister said last night. He was talking about advances under the act. If only $4,9 million is included in the estimates I would like to get the source from which the rest of it has been pledged. But even using the ministers own figures, they seem to me to be demonstrably inaccurate.
What about the $105 million program we were told about in 1958? What about the two thermal plants proposed for New Brunswick? One, of course, is being built and it should be of great assistance to the province. It is

at East Saint John but it is being financed by the provincial government without federal assistance. What about the eight proposed plants for Nova Scotia? There is not one new plant; but assistance, as I have already indicated, was given to increase the capacity of an existing plant at Trenton, Nova Scotia.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding what has been previously said in this house and outside the house, no new thermal power plants are being built in the Atlantic provinces by the present government, and I ask why. The answer seems to me to be quite obvious. It is because no formula has been found by this government to provide for the burning of coal in these plants which the minister said was a condition for federal financial assistance. At the East Saint John, New Brunswick, plant the New Brunswick power commission claimed that oil would save half a million dollars a year. I am not criticizing this decision of the New Brunswick government in any respect because, under the circumstances, they perhaps had no alternative; and as the premier of New Brunswick made quite clear to the Rand commission, oil would be used. That decision, Mr. Speaker, underlines the weakness of the thermal power program put forward by this government.
It seems to me to underline the fact that our formula would have been a more satisfactory one for the Atlantic provinces, because we pledged ourselves as a government to make coal competitive with any other fuel in the production of electricity. That was made perfectly clear, and it was stated categorically by the former minister of public works-the minister from Nova Scotia-in June, 1957. Yet the Prime Minister will not give this house a similar assurance about the East Saint John thermal plant. The result is what we know.
In the face of this attitude, the Prime Minister now claims savings of $20 million in power costs to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in two years. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) has given a figure which does not agree with the Prime Minister's. It is in excess of the actual figure, but he only claims some $9.5 million. We put some questions to the minister in order to ascertain the figures on this point as will be found on pages 2345 and 2346 of Hansard of March 23. According to the minister's answers, the figures were $7.71 million for capital construction and $1.88 million for assistance by way of subventions. That is a far cry from the $20 million mentioned by the Prime Minister in his broadcast. In any event, how can the minister call an advance
3, 1960
Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces of $7.71 million "immediate savings in power costs" when any such advances will be paid back by the provinces, plus interest and service charges. The minister himself boasted when speaking in the House of Commons on January 8, 1958, as may be found on page 3038 of Hansard:
-the amounts of money expended on the construction program will all be refunded with interest, so that this phase of the program is self-liquidating.
Five days later the right hon. gentleman said the construction would involve "no loss whatever to the federal treasury". So the only economy that could possibly be effected is through borrowing from the federal government rather than elsewhere. When we tried to find out by questions where the money for subventions went, and did what we could to find out what savings were involved, we were not able to get that information; we were told it had all gone to the provincial power commission which acted as the agent of the federal government in this matter.
There is something else I should like to deal with, because it is of great importance to the development of the Atlantic provinces. It was touched on by my hon. friend who has just sat down, and it has to do with monetary policy and its effect on the development of the Atlantic region. This is a matter of intense interest to the provincial governments, an interest which has been stimulated and increased as a result of the tight money policy of the present government, and high interest rates.
Over the last two years the provincial governments of the Atlantic region, three of which are supposed to be on such friendly and co-operative terms with the federal government, have been trying at every possible opportunity to get the federal government at least to investigate the effect of monetary policy on regional development. They have pleaded more than once for a more flexible application of monetary policy, and some of them have suggested in their statements that perhaps there might be a differential rate of interest for the Atlantic provinces to take care of their needs. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has stated categorically that this could not be done, and I am not going to quarrel with that financial opinion. Surely, however, there is no justification for the minister's refusal of the repeated requests of the premiers of the Atlantic provinces for an investigation of this matter. The evidence seems clear that the request has been made. The premiers, having found the Minister of Finance completely unresponsive, have decided to go it on their own, and the premier

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces of Nova Scotia, speaking recently in the house of assembly in Halifax, summed up the position by saying:
We had come to the conclusion we could not make any progress in this field-make any progress with the Minister of Finance and his officials- by requesting that something be done, so we were convinced that we would have to document our request with the opinion of a recognized authority in this field.
In the face of this attitude of the Minister of Finance they have taken steps to investigate this matter on a provincial basis. Perhaps, as a result of that investigation, something worth while may be discovered. This is a matter surely, where the federal government could have co-operated when they were first asked to do so by the provincial governments.
I am not suggesting that the Minister of Finance should take any position at this time as to what might be done, but I do suggest- and my suggestion has been supported by the financial editor of the Montreal Gazette- that an investigation should be made. As the editor of the Gazette said-and I quote from his column which appeared, I think, on April 8, 1960:
All (areas) are affected by the expansion or contraction of the money supply. What is wanted are measures which restrain those areas or those industries which require restraint without hurting those which do not.
Then, later:
If it is impossible with present procedures, the maritimes not unreasonably argue, the procedures should be changed.
If the Atlantic provinces now feel that national monetary policy is being applied unfairly to them, not only, perhaps, in the sphere of interest rates but in the availability of money at a fixed rate for the Atlantic provinces; if they feel that-and they do feel it-that will add to their problems; it will add to the grievances of the area, and it is going to make the national application of monetary policy more difficult. I suggest, therefore, that the federal government should have co-operated wholeheartedly with the Atlantic provinces in the kind of examination which was sought. The considerations which I have just mentioned, together with a good many others, surely support the desirability of an inquiry to study this phase of monetary policy with the object of assessing the adverse effects on the Atlantic region of present monetary policy and, perhaps, to relieve any such adverse effects. A study of this kind in which the federal government participated together with the Atlantic provinces would surely have a better chance of making the most constructive kind of recommendations.


If this is now to be done on a provincial basis, it could be better done on a joint cooperative basis.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? I understood him to say that the maritime provinces were seeking an expert opinion which would support regional differences. Have they already secured such an opinion, or are they still seeking it?

They asked a distinguished British economist, Sir Oliver Franks, to undertake the work but I understand' through the press that he regretfully replied that he could not take on the job. They are, no doubt, trying to get an equally distinguished expert to do it in the hope that they may find some solution to this problem.

I had been attempting to analyse some of the problems of the Atlantic region. I come now to the more important question, what to do about it. The arguments on that, in part at least, are found in the amendment, on which we shall shortly be voting, moved by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate which calls for a comprehensive and planned program of federal assistance for the Atlantic provinces. The amendment then recites a number of elements which, in our view, ought to be considered at the earliest possible time as part of such a comprehensive and planned program. I emphasize the words "planned" and ."comprehensive" as opposed to ad hoc, unrelated and temporary expedients.
This emphasis that I venture to place on planning and co-ordination received strong support from the Halifax ChYonicle-Herald in an admirable discussion of Atlantic problems and plans in an article entitled "A Blueprint for Atlantic Advance". I might quote one sentence from that blueprint, Mr. Speaker:
-ad hoc provisions... do not provide the solution to the basic economic problem which confronts the Atlantic region of Canada with such magnitude today.
I know that to inaugurate any program of this kind the Canadian people as a whole would willingly accept obligations that might follow from such a program, provided that the public funds in question were spent constructively and in ways which would improve facilities and stimulate income and employment. My own view on this has been

made known already in this session, when I said that the wealthier parts of this country will have to accept obligations, perhaps in a way they have not in the past, to the economically weaker and less developed parts of the country and to help solve their special problems.
The Canso causeway is a prototype of this kind of planned, creative project. This program would require special capital assistance for the Atlantic provinces, a capital assistance program which should not be regarded in any sense as a handout but as a constructive method of balancing in that area what has been done in other regions of Canada. In fact, it would help balance at least, federal programs in other parts of Canada such as the St. Lawrence seaway and the trans-Canada pipe line which, when they are carried out- and some of them have been-will certainly help other regions more than they will help the Atlantic provinces.
Moreover, it seems to me it would be desirable to establish special administrative arrangements to operate such an Atlantic capital projects program. I should like to suggest for consideration that the industrial development bank should be used for this special regional purpose, even if it might require an amendment to the legislation setting up that bank.
Certainly the establishment of more secondary industries in the Atlantic provinces is essential, although we know in the past this has been hindered, first, by transportation costs and the difficulties arising from those costs and second, because of the fact that the market-although it is growing-is not big enough to absorb the present products of those regions. Because of the desirability of this new expansion we are obliged then to seek new means and not merely try to improve on the old methods that we have been following in the past.
Among the new means which we advocate in this amendment are the provision of fiscal incentives to encourage new industries to establish in areas where old industries are declining. This method would be fully justified in the coal areas of Nova Scotia for the purpose of easing the social and economic impact of changes, when they have to take place of reduced production, if it has to take place, and of cut-backs and of mine closures. Even if a solution-perhaps from the recommendations of the Rand commission -can be found that will increase or at least stabilize coal production, nevertheless it will remain essential to devise measures to expand and diversify employment opportunities not only in those coal areas but throughout the Atlantic provinces generally. That is

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces why we make in our amendment two suggestions, namely the capital projects program which I mentioned, and the provision of fiscal incentives to new industries, which I think should be considered now by this government.
It would be wrong to rely entirely on accelerated development of existing resources or on stimulation of secondary industries. Great benefits to the Atlantic provinces would accrue economically from the discovery of entirely new and presently unknown resources, as was pointed out in the Gordon commission report a few years ago. That is a more long term endeavour, but it certainly in our view should not be neglected.
Therefore we advocate the intensification of federal activity in this field to complete our knowledge, which is not now complete, of the resources of the Atlantic area. As a party we made a policy statement on this matter in 1958 and perhaps I can put it on record. It is as follows:
The Liberal party, with a view to accelerating the economic development of the Atlantic provinces stands for a policy of special federal effort to explore, survey, map, measure and make generally available up-to-date knowledge of the natural resources of the Atlantic provinces, so as to bring about speedier maximum use of the natural wealth of the Atlantic area, thereby raising the standard of prosperity in that part of Canada.
In addition, we attach at this time great importance to measures leading to a more efficient use of land. A principal cause of lower income levels is the relatively larger number of persons engaged in subsistence farming, fishing and logging. The low incomes prevailing in such subsistence occupations depress the average earnings in the whole area. A report attached to the Gordon commission, entitled "Some regional aspects of Canada's economic development" points out:
If these sectors of the Atlantic regional economy are eliminated for purposes of calculation, the disparity in average annual earnings is lessened considerably . . . annual earnings in the primary aspects of farming, fishing and forestry were about 50 per cent of the Ontario average.
Therefore, a more efficient use of these basic land resources would be a direct method of increasing standards of living in that area; and I believe that the successful prosecution of this objective should receive much greater governmental attention than it has.
These are some of the things which we put in the amendment which is now before the house. Very often when we on this side speak we are asked the question from the other side, "what would you do?" Well these are the measures that we would support in

Federal Aid to Atlantic Provinces any program to strengthen the economy of the Atlantic provinces and improve income levels:
1.	A capital projects program.
2.	Fiscal incentives to stimulate private enterprise.
3.	New efforts to discover new resources in the Atlantic provinces.
4.	A more efficient use of land resources.
5.	An inquiry into the regional effects of national, fiscal, monetary and economic policies.
6.	Adjustments in freight rates and improvement of transportation facilities.
That is what we would do, Mr. Speaker.

I rise on a grievance. I should like to raise a matter which has caused widespread concern throughout the country during the past few weeks, and understandably so. I am referring to the situation caused by the apparent failure of the government's housing program for 1960.

When housing legislation came before us for discussion in this chamber in February and March of this year we were told by the minister responsible that the government planned to reduce housebuilding in 1960 as compared with 1959 and 1958. At that time the minister said the government's objective was 125,000 starts in 1960 as compared with
141,000	in 1959 and 164,000 in 1958. Some of us on this side of the house tried to point out that because of the tight money and high interest rates caused by government fiscal and monetary policy it would be unlikely that more than 100,000 starts would be made in 1960.
It is not my intention to repeat here arguments which were used at that time. It is common knowledge that the government, through its conversion loan of 1958 and its huge deficits, boosted interest rates to unprecedented levels for government borrowings which, in turn, boosted interest rates on all borrowing for building operations. The results of this policy, which led to higher interest rates, have had the effect of knocking the banks completely out of house building. Only 19 loans were made by the chartered banks in the first quarter of 1960 as compared with 3,327 in the first quarter of 1959. Government policy, resulting as it has in higher interest rates throughout the economy, has also had a most detrimental effect on lending for house building by the approved lenders-

Mr. Speaker, in the light of this statement by a senior member of this government that the construction of 146,000 houses created 400,000 jobs, quite apart from the other businesses referred to such as the supplying of lumber, furniture, appliances and so forth, what possible justification can there be for this government to sit on its hands with hundreds of thousands of our people unemployed. Statistics show that in no field is there greater unemployment than among residential construction workers. Yet the government sits there day in and day out, like one of Dickens' characters, hoping that something will turn up.
All winter the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) kept telling us, "Do it now, don't wait for spring". A month ago, during the budget presentation, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) urged us, "Don't worry now, wait until spring". The time for action by this government in respect of the 1960 housing program is long overdue. Here we have the government, by its own statement, having within its power the ability to create an extra 200,000 jobs, and yet stubbornly refusing to do so.
Parliament has already approved $500 million for direct lending to bolster the housing program, yet this government refuses to act. Its refusal leaves one with only one conclusion, namely that they are holding the

bulk of these millions approved by parliament to be poured into the economy prior to the next general election. This sort of action on the part of a national government, if true, is deplorable and certainly by their actions they are leaving themselves open to this criticism.
If there are other reasons why the government is refusing to use these dollars, let them come forward and say so. Actually, while they propose lending $150 million to $175 million this year, the government will be receiving an estimated $110 million in interest and mortgage payments. This means, of course, that while the fund is not a revolving one, the additional net lending proposed will be only $40 million to $65 million.
During the housing debate much was said about the 82,000 units carried over from last year which remained to be completed. The National House Builders Association release, as far back as April 4, estimated that no more than 10 per cent of the labour required to complete these 82,000 units remained to be done. It is obvious to all of us that loans being applied for now, with the usual administrative time lag, will not result in any real employment for several weeks or even months.
In view of these circumstances, I think the government should act now. With their many experts I am sure they are very much aware of the causes and results of this bogging down of house construction in 1960. In the light of present circumstances I think they should re-assess the situation at once and show the public that they are determined that the rate of house construction will be increased so as to ensure the provision of adequate housing for our people and to show the Canadian people that they, the government, are aware of the relationship between the number of Canadians unemployed and the rate of house construction in Canada.
There are many aspects of housing that could and perhaps should be dealt with at this time. There are internal problems within the industry itself which add to builders' costs and are simply passed along to the buyer. I believe the government has a responsibility to prevent violent fluctuations in the industry that result in a higher cost for houses. However, as I have indicated, we have had a rather extensive debate on housing earlier this year.
I will close by reminding hon. members that housing starts have averaged 138,000 yearly for the past five years. The government has set 125,000 as this year's objective. Results to date clearly indicate that this minimum objective of the government will not be met. The need for proper housing remains great among many of our people. Great quantities

of building materials lie waiting in inventory. Residential construction workers stand by unemployed and waiting. Surely the house construction industry and hundreds of thousands of our people do not have to stand by waiting for a sag in the Canadian economy that might have the effect of making more mortgage money available for houses. I believe that human need should have priority and I do not believe there is any justification for the government sitting around with almost $500 million up its sleeve while our unemployed walk the streets.

I found that this lack of action was spreading consternation amongst the builders in my riding. I talked with one builder who planned to construct 100 homes this year but because of the lack of available funds he has had to cancel the whole project.
Now some two or three weeks ago I had occasion in this house to read a letter from a disillusioned former supporter of this government. As I went around my riding during the last two or three weeks I found that there were quite a number of former supporters of this government who had joined the ranks of the disillusioned. Not too long ago I attended a meeting of the northeastern Ontario development association in which the civic leaders from all the northeastern parts of Ontario took part. They were meeting to try to find how they could develop that particular section of northern Ontario. They discussed various ways and means, but each and every amendment they discussed crashed on the same rocks. How was the money going to be made available? How were they going to get the money for the construction of

homes, for small industries and so forth? This is something that is very keenly felt in that area right now because for some 18 or 20 years the Porcupine camp was at a standstill. It has only been within the last two years or so that the camp has started to come alive. In fact, during the last two years there was more construction in the Timmins area than there had been in the previous 20 years.
And under Conservative rule.

Unfortunately this hope that came into being in that area has come to a sorry halt this year. Everybody with whom I talked wanted to know what the trouble was. They were of the opinion that $500 million had been made available for housing and wanted to know why that money was not available. When I told them that the government's stated intention was to use only a very small portion of that money they asked the same question that I asked in the house. Unfortunately, whether or not it was for the same reason, they did not get an answer. I did not know the answer because I was not able to find out in the house.
I would suggest, and this is just my personal opinion as a result of talking to a number of people over the last few weeks, that if the government does not care about the public or about the unemployed in this particular field, then they had better start to care about their own future. This unfortunate situation in the construction field seems to have started the moment the former minister of public works left that office. I do not know whether or not there is any connection between the two events. It seemed, when the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) was minister of public works he was the only minister in the cabinet who was really doing a job. When we take a good look at the housing situation today, even though the international situation may be serious, I think that for the good of this country we had better call him back to his job at public works.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. M. T. McDonald (Hamilton South):
speechtext:
I should like to make a few comments on this grievance. I cannot agree with the Liberal or C.C.F. members, but there is one point upon which I must commend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker). I refer to limited dividend mortgage money. Some few years ago the Liberal party started this Liberal dividend provision and from 1946 to 1957 they put $58 million into limited dividend projects. From June 10, 1957 until December 31, 1959 this government put $115 million into this market, and I think they should be commended for their action.
Suggested Increase in Housing Program
However, I am a little disturbed at the amount of loans that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is allowing private enterprise in their efforts to help the people in the income bracket below $3,600 to finance housing projects. Before the private investor had to put up 10 per cent of his own money and the government provided the remaining 90 per cent. The private investor was allowed to make 5 per cent on his money. A lot of private lenders went into this type of project, even though they might have purchased government bonds. They were shouldering their responsibilities. I would hope the Minister of Public Works would look at this provision a little more closely in the future. In 1957 the minister of finance, Walter Harris, had a little report on housing and I should like to quote from that report:
Housing construction is expected to drop fairly markedly below the high levels of the two previous years.
This statement was made just before the election and the two cups of coffee budget. We did not hear of the great Liberal party pouring money into the housing market to help the builders of the country. If this government had not put $150 million into the housing market in July, 1957, 75 per cent of the small builders in this country would have been bankrupt. It was the direct responsibility of the Liberal party before the budget of March, 1957 when they knew the condition of the housing industry in the country and failed to meet their responsibility. They must accept the responsibility for their failure to take action.
This government has done a lot in the housing field in the past three years and more remains to be done.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In view of the fact that the hon. member is dealing with the past, may I remind the house that this is a narrow subject with which we are dealing. This grievance relates to the administration of the housing act passed and amended by parliament this year. It does not deal with the past but with the present, as I understand the grievance. I think more hon. members will have an opportunity to speak if the discussion is kept to that narrow range.

Thank you for calling me to order, Mr. Speaker. I hope I can get back on the track. This government raised the amount of insured N.H.A. moneys from $4 million to $6 million. Unlike the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) I am a little concerned about the inactivity of the lending institutions in the country who make available money at 6| per cent. It is all well and good, as indicated before, to say that they can collect bonds and get quite
3530	HOUSE OF
Suggested Increase in Housing Program a bit of money, but it is the people's money that the banks and lending institutions have. It is up to them to take a long range view at future housing and construction in Canada. I think it is about time they shouldered a little bit more responsibility in this field.
When speaking in this house a few months ago on the subject of housing I indicated that the government should get out of the direct lending business. I feel this is something the government should do in a long range program. They should stay in the field of insured N.H.A. lending but it is the responsibility of banks, trust companies and other financial institutions in a private enterprise system to be active in direct lending. I do not say the government should get out of this type of business immediately but should stay in it until the rough period is over and then get out. The lending institutions should take a longer ranged view and possibly shoulder their responsibilities more adequately.
I think that the present Minister of Public Works is attempting to meet his responsibilities squarely. I know that I have had complaints, but then we have complaints about everything. I have no doubt that hon. members opposite received complaints too when they sat on the government side of the house. I believe that the minister has put forward a direct policy. I am sure he has not had too many complaints because the people have accepted this. The builders are in a bad way, it is true, but it is due to the high cost of land and the lack of services. One could name a thousand other reasons. I am sure that the minister and this government will take the proper action that is necessary to help the Canadian housing industry and will not do what the Liberals did in March of 1957.

Mr. Speaker, among the many grievances which the Canadian people have against the present government undoubtedly one of the most fiercely debated throughout the country is the present administration of the housing act. As you stated, Mr. Speaker, we recently amended this act and following these amendments regulations were passed and directions given as to the future administration of the legislation.
Throughout Canada and more specifically in my area of northern Canada it has been found that the administration of the act works a hardship in many cases. If there was ever a project which had social significance in this country it was the housing project promoted by the former government over a period of many years. The hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland) has adduced enlightening statistics which indicate that home


construction has been reduced by 45 per cent under the administration of the present government. This is due to many causes but the fault rests primarily with the government. The reasons arise in large part from the regulations put into effect following the amendments of 1960.
Another reason why this grievance is exceedingly important to the people of Canada is because the unemployment situation has been aggravated by and reflects a falling off of residential home construction. This has affected my area wherein we have prosperous mines. Unemployment there has doubled between March of 1958 and March of 1960. I dare say that approximately 80 per cent of those who find themselves in the doubled numbers of unemployed in my area were employed in the construction industry. Construction activity in northern Ontario has decreased at a serious rate.
For the two reasons I have advanced I am sure that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and the government as a whole will listen to the voices of hon. members who have spoken in this debate and will bring about certain changes in the recently imposed regulations which have brought about the disaster to which I referred. I am not alone in drawing this matter to the attention of the government. This trend has been observed and commented upon by several hon. members and many alert citizens.
I would like to quote from a newspaper article containing a report of a recent meeting between northern Ontario municipalities to discuss this grave problem of home construction and its effect on the economic situation of various areas. Unfortunately the article happened to be written in French but of course with the translation system with which we are favoured all hon. members will be able to follow. This article appeared in the newspaper Le Devoir and reads:
(Translation):
Allow me to quote from an article which appeared in Le Droit for April 29, under the following heading:
Sudbury files the same application as Kapus-kasing.
And the article goes on to say:
Unless certain changes are made in the National Housing Act, heavy losses are in the offing for the building industry in the Sudbury area.
Tuesday night, the Sudbury city council unanimously passed a resolution urging the federal government to raise by $1,000 the salary ceiling for qualifying for mortgage loans through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
(Text):
This action by members of municipalities in northern Ontario clearly illustrates the impasse which the housing industry has

reached there. Housing has been reduced by 45 per cent. The statistics reveal drastic declines. I am sure this government will assume some responsibility in this important field and give an incentive to the housing industry.
One problem created by the new regulations is the maximum salary figure of $5,000 in relation to obtaining direct loans. Miners are confronted with a problem with respect to the bonuses they receive from time to time. These bonuses vary greatly in relation to certain jobs in the mining industry. A miner therefore has to report that he receives a variable income which will fluctuate widely from year to year.
In the mining industry you have workers in the mines and smelters. Let us assume that a smelter worker earning between $4,400 and $4,500 obtains a loan from this government assist in securing a home for himself and his family. But a miner, a mucker as we call him in the district of Sudbury, who works just a few miles away and who is considered for every purpose on the same social level as the furnace puncher or smelter man, if he is making $5,100 he cannot obtain from the government the service which his fellow workers can obtain. That is because his pay is slightly more than the others, possibly because his work is more dangerous or is heavier. We have set ways and means to enable a person in this country to obtain the service of this government at a figure of $5,000, and I say this is wrong.
Further, I realize that we have been called repeaters, but for 15 or 20 years it has been repeated to me that the cost of living in northern Ontario is higher than elsewhere. That is true because of the cost of transportation of materials and goods, and it is also true for other various reasons. The cost of public works is much more in northern Ontario than in other places in Canada and the province of Ontario because the cost of living is much higher. Therefore the pay must follow the cost of living in some way and we find a rather fair rate of wages in northern Ontario. So that this system of using a level of $5,000 creates a situation in this province and elsewhere in Canada where the salary of a regional director of a company of some major store, for instance, in one area is, say, $4,800 and therefore this person under the regulations can obtain a service from the government which provides a loan so he can build a home. In my riding a worker, not a district manager of a store but a worker, cannot get a loan under the regulations of this government and for this reason it is obvious he has a grievance owing to the most harsh and difficult situation in the area I represent.
Suggested Increase in Housing Program
We have seen other statutes being administered with variations from area to area. We see this in the laws of the federal government and in the industrial standards act of the province of Ontario where minimum wages are zoned by areas. The minimum standards act of Ontario does not declare the same minimum wage for northern Ontario as it does for some other sections of that province.
To be fair to all these people in Canada who are on the same social level but possibly do not receive the same pay cheque on Saturdays on account of the region in which they live and on account of the cost of living in their respective area, I would like to say that they find themselves in a position where they cannot obtain this government service and that they have a clear grievance against this government. The government has introduced an absolute arbitrary figure with which they distinguish between the citizens who can obtain the service of this government and the citizens who can not. In taking such an arbitrary figure they have created in my area especially, great disadvantages.
I have a letter here which I think should convince the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker). I have received information through a letter which is in the form of a petition. It is not from an ordinary citizen in my riding but it comes through the committee of the unemployment insurance commission in my area. Hon. members know that the unemployment insurance commission has a committee which studies ways and means of putting men to work. Here we have this government after passing this new legislation being criticized by sections of the administration of this country and by sections of the unemployment insurance commission, the committee of which meets with laymen to discuss ways and means of putting men to work. I would like to quote a paragraph of this letter for the benefit of the Minister of Public Works. The letter is on the letterhead of the unemployment insurance commission, national employment service, and the address is 152 Elm street east, Sudbury, Ontario. Apparently they had passed a resolution at the meeting of this committee, and one paragraph of this letter reads as follows:
-to petition the federal government to eliminate the premium and bonus factors from the maximum income level required to qualify for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans and that they consider basic pay only.
I am sure the Minister of Public Works has received many directions or demands similar to this one.
As I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I trust that this government through the Minister of
