speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have ten minutes in which to reply and I would like to say in reply to the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland) that his figures do not include any loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation because they covered the first three months of the year, and as such of course they are greatly down on the average for last year. If the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans had been included in the estimate of 73,000 starts for the year 1960, then we would have had 15,000 more starts added to that. If the areas under 5,000 population had been taken into consideration we would have had average figures of 125,000 starts for this year.
I do appreciate what hon. members have said, that there are a great many aggravating situations resulting from the necessity of placing a ceiling on the loans; in other words, to determine by income those who will get loans. But let me first deal very briefly with unemployment. I can assure you that so far our housing policy has done nothing but improve the situation of employment. At the beginning of this year there were 82,000 homes in the process of construction, and as the hon. member will see by looking at the figures, the highlights, up to the end of March there were 22,000 homes completed in the dominion all of which created employment. Employment will fall off so far as home building is concerned pretty soon, but in the meantime the predictions are, according to one of the most authoritative journals, the Canadian Bank of Commerce journal, that the only significant decline in construction this year would seem to be that of housing. Other construction, as we have heard predicted, could be substantially up.
It is a very easy thing to keep on pumping one third of a billion dollars a year into the economy. I would be a popular minister with the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) if I repeated that performance every year. We have pumped into housing in less than


three years nearly $1 billion with the result that we made the market a most difficult market in which to borrow money because of the tremendous borrowings necessary to finance housing. In other words, we helped to spoil the lending market. In addition to this, we are now out of the recession and on our way back to prosperity and, as hon. members will see as the weeks go by, unemployment figures will go down in a very radical way. Therefore, where would we find help in the event of another recession?
We should not be able to go back to housing in the same way as we could in 1957. If there was ever a year, as we come out of the recession and as the construction figures in every other part of our economy go up, this is the year to cut back on our housing. I admit that I share the disappointment of other hon. members that the banks have not participated in the program. Last year we had 15,000 loans from this source; this year, so far, they have not provided 25 loans. Of course, the figure of 15,000 was for the whole of the year. However, we have put the question to hon. members of the opposition: would you allow the interest rate to be raised to 6f per cent in order to bring the banks back into this field? The answer has always been, no. Therefore this is a situation which it is difficult to improve on.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
At the end of my speech.
The builders have not had any loans thus far from us. Never in the years 1958, or 1959, have the builders received anything by way of loans from the government of Canada except by way of winter works loans, and that does not happen until the fall. Thus the complaint that the builders are not getting money from us in the spring is not well founded.
It is true we have cut our program from $337 million to $175 million which will enable us to have between 17,000 and 18,000 starts. So great is the demand for direct government loans that we have been forced to find some way of letting out these loans, and the fairest way is to help those who need help most, namely the man of small income and his family. Even with a ceiling of $5,000 for the ordinary man with two children, $5,200 for the man with three children, $5,400 for the man with four children and $5,600 for the man with five children, we are going to have a hard time making this $175 million last. The demand for loans from us is tremendous. We were only open for business from April 6, but we have already received 2,000 applications, and it is going to be difficult to make the

money last to the end of the year. If we were to raise the ceiling to $6,000-and no one would like that better than I would; I hate to hear complaints from the hon. member from Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) and other members, because I know perfectly well that because of the necessity of letting our money out in this limited way certain people are suffering-if we were to raise this ceiling to $6,000 at the present time we would run out of money by the end of June, because it is a fact that the banks are not in this program.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
When I am through. The banks are not in it. They have completely dropped out, and the approved lenders have been very slow in getting in. However, we expect that the conventional lenders will be back just as they were before, and it will please hon. members to know that although I cannot be exact about anything I am going to suggest that the figures I gave several months ago will, even without the banks, be almost achieved this year; that is 85,000 conventional loans or non-N.H.A. loans; 20,000 loans from approved lenders, because as the weeks go by the approved lenders are getting back into the market and we are still hopeful we shall get
20,000	starts from the approved lenders. Thus one arrives at a figure of 105,000 starts. Added to that there are 15,000 starts by way of direct housing loans, and 3,000 starts on limited dividend projects, making another 18,000 and completing a total for this year of 123,000 as compared with my earlier prediction of 125,000.
So to my friends of faint hope may I say: consider, with us, the problem we have to face. Do hon. members opposite want the government to go on lending one third of a billion dollars a year, bearing in mind the difficulty there is in getting money and the fact that money raised by the government means the exclusion of other people from the means of borrowing? We are trying to do the best we can. We are trying to hand out our money to the people who need it most, and if we had more money we would lend it to people in higher income brackets. Let us not be fainthearted. The approved lenders who did not have this matter to consider until the spring are now getting back into the market. For our part we are going to lend every cent we have to those people with incomes of $5,000 or less, and before the end of the year hon. members may be better pleased than they are at the present time. I can also predict that the construction figures in which we are all so vitally interested will be as high, if not higher than in any other 79951-0-223

Will the hon. gentleman permit a question? In stating that he would like to be fair, has the minister given any consideration to establishing a scale for maximum earnings which would vary according to areas and in that way be definitely fair?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: That is a very good suggestion. There is a very great variation, particularly in the Nickel Belt where they get such big bonuses. At the present time while we have this policy we are bound to take care of the people whose income is $5,000 or less. Does that answer the question?
Would the minister permit a further question? I was wondering on what basis he gives the house the figure of 85,000 starts outside N.H.A. lending. What figures has he to substantiate that estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The figures we had last year, what we called conventional loans.
